pub fn connect(host: String) { ... }  // exported
fn internal_retry() { ... }  // private — no annotation needed

options.name: Keep S18: private-by-default + per-item pub
options.detail: No change. Beginners never accidentally expose internals. Boilerplate grows proportionally with exports, not inversely. The safety argument is unchanged from the original ratification. The correct response to a module with 18 public items is to ask whether it has too many exports, not to flip the default.

options.name: Public-by-default + explicit private
options.detail: Every item is exported unless marked `priv` or `private`. Lowers the pub-count for export-heavy modules. Beginners accidentally expose internals; the 'safe by default' principle (I1 analog for encapsulation) is broken. The owner declined this in the S18 ratification notes.
options.code:
// proposed public-by-default:
fn send(msg: String) { ... }      // public — no annotation
fn connect(host: String) { ... }  // public — no annotation
priv fn retry() { ... }           // must opt into private

options.name: Add a file-scope marker (#scope_file / pub:)
options.detail: Keep private-by-default but allow a section marker that flips the default for everything below it in the file. Owner explicitly declined this form at S18 (positional grouping dictates file structure). It is Jai-style grouped visibility under a different name.
options.code:
// proposed section marker (owner declined this form at S18):
pub:
fn send(msg: String) { ... }      // public by position
fn connect(host: String) { ... }  // public by position
priv:
fn retry() { ... }                // private by position

comparisons.note: Go uses public-by-default via capitalization: exported identifiers start with an uppercase letter. Simple but tied to naming; no keyword for visibility.
comparisons.code:
func Send(msg string) {}     // exported (capital S)
func retry() {}              // unexported (lowercase)

comparisons.note: Rust uses private-by-default + `pub`, same as S18. The `pub(crate)` and `pub(super)` scopes are considered a strength, not a boilerplate problem.
comparisons.code:
pub fn send(msg: &str) {}
fn retry() {}  // private — no annotation

decisions.comment: We will keep private by default, per item pub, BUT allow public/private scope markers. I want a new decision open to compare syntax options for the marker though

decisions.title: Ship user-authored derives + typed reflection (Epoch 3 exit criterion)?
decisions.gist: Libraries need to author derives (like #[Serialize], #[Codable]) using a typed reflection API. The Epoch 3 exit criterion includes this. The v1 ceiling is already ratified: reflection + derives only, no arbitrary macros. This is the umbrella proceed/kill gate; D-METAREFLECT1 (read API) and D-METADERIVE1 (output) are sub-decisions that open only if this passes.
decisions.explainer: Today only builtin derives exist. User-authored derives require two things: (1) a typed reflection API that lets comptime code inspect a type's fields, types, and markers (D-METAREFLECT1); and (2) a mechanism for derive output to re-enter the compiler and be sema-checked (D-METADERIVE1). D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies the architecture rule (output must re-enter sema, not bypass it). The v1 ceiling (no arbitrary macros) is the I8 guard: derives are a single, scoped metaprogramming job; general macros would be a second surface that can do the same job. Deferring blocks any library that needs Serialize, ORM field mapping, or any type-driven code generation until post-v1.
decisions.story: I'm writing a serialization library. I want to derive Serialize on any user struct automatically — inspect its fields at comptime and emit the encode/decode implementation. I should not need to hardcode this into the compiler.

options.name: Ship user derives + typed reflection within the ratified ceiling
options.detail: Approve opening D-METAREFLECT1 and D-METADERIVE1. Delivers the Epoch 3 exit criterion; enables third-party derive libraries (Serialize, ORM, validation); keeps the ceiling at reflection+derives (no arbitrary macros). D-CTCODEGEN1's architecture constraint (output re-enters sema) applies.

options.name: Builtin derives only; no user-authored derives
options.detail: Keep derives as a closed set in the compiler. No reflection API, no derive output mechanism. Library authors cannot add new derives; every new derive requires a compiler PR. Blocks the serialization, ORM, and validation library ecosystem.

options.name: Defer to post-Epoch 3
options.detail: Treat user derives as post-v1. Epoch 3 ships without a derive authoring API. Third-party serialization/ORM libraries cannot work without manual impl. Re-evaluate after the runtime, async, and other Epoch 3 exits are done.

comparisons.note: Rust derive macros are proc-macros that receive a TokenStream and emit a TokenStream — powerful but operate on syntax trees, not typed reflection. Jet's typed reflection API is safer and simpler.
Swift's Codable is a compiler-synthesized protocol conformance — a builtin derive only. Third-party derives are impossible; every new derive requires a Swift compiler change.

decisions.title: Reflection read API: what does a type expose to comptime code?
decisions.gist: User-authored derives need to inspect types at comptime. This decision specifies what a type exposes: field names, field types, markers, ordering, and privacy. It is the read side of the metaprogramming system; the write side (output mechanism) is D-METADERIVE1. Opens only if D-USERDERIVE1 passes.
decisions.explainer: The reflection API must be read-only (no mutation of type structure at comptime), privacy-respecting (private fields not visible to derives from other packages), and typed (fields expose their Jet types, not strings). The minimum to author a Serialize derive is: iterate fields, get each field's name (String) and type (Type), and read its markers. Methods, generics, and inheritance reflection can come in a later phase. The API surface must be expressible inside the existing `comptime { }` block and `$` splice system. New syntax is not required — it is a stdlib comptime API, not a new language construct. I8 is satisfied: this is the only mechanism to inspect a type at comptime.
decisions.story: In my derive_Serialize comptime function, I call `T.fields()` and get back an array of field descriptors. I loop over them, read each field's name and type, and splice in the encode call for that field. I never see private fields from other packages.

options.name: Read-only typed API: fields + types + markers (v1 minimum)
options.detail: Expose `T.fields() -> [FieldDesc]` where each FieldDesc has `.name() -> String`, `.type() -> Type`, `.markers() -> [Marker]`, and `.is_pub() -> Bool`. Private fields from other packages are invisible. No method reflection, no generic-param reflection in v1. Minimum surface to ship Serialize, Codable, ORM mapping.

options.name: Opaque types: no reflection API
options.detail: Types are opaque to comptime code; no field introspection. Derives must be hardcoded in the compiler. Blocks D-USERDERIVE1; makes this ballot moot. Listed for completeness.
options.code:
// no T.fields() available
// derive_Serialize cannot be written by a library author

options.name: Rich reflection: fields + methods + generics + annotations
options.detail: Expose method reflection (`T.methods()`), generic parameter reflection (`T.type_params()`), and arbitrary annotation inspection in v1. More powerful but much larger API surface to stabilize. Methods are not needed for any known derive use case; adds complexity before the simpler path proves out.

comparisons.note: Zig's `@typeInfo` returns a tagged union describing a type's fields, decls, and layout. Read-only; used by comptime functions to drive codegen. Close to option A.
Java's reflection is runtime-based, not comptime. It exposes fields, methods, annotations, and generics — option C's scope — but at a runtime cost and without type safety at the call site.

decisions.title: Derive output: emit Jet source via $ splice, re-parsed and sema-checked?
decisions.gist: User-authored derives need a way to emit code. D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies that output must re-enter lexer/parser/sema (never bypass it). This decision fixes the surface: the `$` splice inside `comptime { }` is the output mechanism. Opens only if D-USERDERIVE1 passes.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 forbids derives from emitting Rust directly or manipulating the AST in-place — all output must be Jet source that re-enters the front end. The `$` splice already exists for comptime value injection. The question is whether derive output is the same `$` splice mechanism (extended to emit function/impl blocks) or a separate API (typed AST builder). A typed AST builder is a second mechanism for emitting code — I8 violation. The `$` splice path means all derive errors appear in Jet source terms, not in opaque AST operations (I2/I3 compliant). The main risk is that splicing multi-line impl blocks requires the splice to carry statement-level fragments, not just expressions — a small extension to the existing mechanic.
decisions.story: My derive_Serialize function builds up a String of Jet source for the encode/decode methods, then splices it in with `${ ... }`. The parser re-reads it; sema checks the types; if I made a mistake, the error points at the generated Jet, not at rustc output.

options.name: $ splice emits Jet source fragments, re-parsed and sema-checked
options.detail: Extend the existing `$` splice to carry statement- and item-level Jet source (not just expressions). The emitted text re-enters the lexer and parser exactly as user-written Jet would. Sema sees the expanded code; errors appear in Jet source terms. One mechanism for comptime output; I8 satisfied; I2/I3 satisfied.

options.name: Typed AST builder API
options.detail: Derives call a builder API (`ImplBlock.new()`, `.add_method()`, etc.) that constructs a typed AST node directly. No string parsing; type-safe at the builder call sites. A second mechanism for emitting code alongside the `$` splice — I8 tension. Builder API surface must be designed, stabilized, and versioned separately.

options.name: Defer derive output mechanism
options.detail: Approve D-USERDERIVE1 and D-METAREFLECT1 but leave the output mechanism open. Reflection ships; derives cannot emit code yet. Partial; blocks the actual derive use cases; not a useful intermediate state.

comparisons.note: Rust proc-macros receive and emit `TokenStream` — effectively source text in token form, re-parsed by the compiler. The `quote!` macro is the ergonomic surface. Jet's `$` splice is the same concept with Jet syntax.
Zig comptime functions return types directly — a typed approach closer to option B. No string emission; the comptime function is the mechanism. Works because Zig's type system is the API surface.

decisions.title: Should core reactivity (auto-updating dependents) be baked into Jet's evaluation model, or remain a library?
decisions.gist: D-REACT1 already decided: reactivity is a library/signal mechanism, not a language primitive. This reopens that decision. The question is whether dependent values should re-evaluate automatically at the language level (spreadsheet-style) or whether the reactive graph lives entirely in user space via a library. This gates every other reactive-UI card in this batch.
decisions.explainer: Amends D-REACT1. If core-semantic reactivity is adopted, it changes how assignments and data-flow work throughout the language — every cell/value becomes potentially reactive, which has massive implications for mental model, predictability, and interop with the rest of the type system. If it stays a library, reactivity is opt-in and explicit, matching I1 (safe/predictable defaults) and I8 (one canonical mechanism — the signal library). The following cards all gate on this decision: D-REACTUI1 (reactive-ui-stack), D-MOTION1 (motion-as-state), typed-styles, ownable-components. Decide this first before any of those can proceed.
decisions.story: I want to write a UI where changing a value automatically updates everything that depends on it — like a spreadsheet, but in compiled code. The question is whether that auto-update behavior is built into the language itself or comes from a library I import.

options.name: Library / signals (keep D-REACT1)
options.detail: Reactivity lives in a stdlib signals library. Dependents re-evaluate only when explicitly using signal APIs. Predictable evaluation order, no hidden re-runs, I1-safe — the reactive graph is always visible. This is the current decision.

options.name: Core evaluation semantics (reactive cells)
options.detail: Assignment to a 'cell' in a reactive scope automatically propagates to all dependents, like a spreadsheet. Elegant for UI but hides re-evaluation, makes reasoning about when code runs harder, and complicates the ownership/borrow model. Large blast radius — touches assignment semantics, closures, and codegen.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Block all reactive-UI cards until a later milestone. Avoids committing to a design before the UI stack architecture is clearer. Delays the entire reactive-UI roadmap.

options.name: #Reactive scope marker (new — owner question 2026-06-26)
options.detail: Add a `#Reactive` compiler-blessed scope marker. Inside `#Reactive { ... }` or `#Reactive fn`, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions — the library handles the graph. Outside the marker, code is purely imperative. Desugars to a library call: `reactive_scope(|| { ... })`. Exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works. I8-safe: one way to opt into reactive behavior. No new evaluation semantics — `core.reactive` provides all the machinery. Both spellings work: `#Reactive fn update(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (function always re-runs when sources change) and `fn update { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (block-level scope). Closer to Option A (library) than Option B (core semantics) — only a scope marker is added to the language.

comparisons.note: Compiler-level reactivity: `$:` labels make assignments reactive at compile time. Elegant but it is a compiler transform, not runtime semantics — and it only applies inside Svelte components.
comparisons.code: $: doubled = count * 2;

comparisons.note: Library-level signals via property wrappers. Reactive but explicit opt-in — closer to option A.
comparisons.code:
@Published var count = 0
let doubled = $count.map { $0 * 2 }

decisions.title: Should Jet define a render-target backend-trait seam now, before any concrete UI backend exists?
decisions.gist: A render-target abstraction would let one UI description compile to web, native, embedded, or TUI by swapping a backend trait. The question is whether to define that seam now (before backends exist), build one target first and generalize later, or defer entirely. Research recommends deciding the seam early to avoid lock-in.
decisions.explainer: This is prerequisite architecture for D-REACTUI1. If the seam is wrong, migrating later forces breaking changes to every UI-layer API. Defining the trait shape now does not require implementing any backend — just agreeing on what a backend must provide (layout, paint, event dispatch). Gated on D-REACTCORE1 for the reactive-event model. Touches the typed-styles card (styles must be expressible in backend-agnostic terms). Bundle-risk: each target (web/WASM, native/GPU, embedded/framebuffer, TUI/ANSI) has very different constraints — the seam must be thin enough to not over-specify.
decisions.story: I want to write a UI once and ship it to the web, desktop, and terminal without rewriting the view layer. That means the core UI logic can't assume any one rendering backend.

options.name: Define the backend-trait seam now
options.detail: Agree on the minimum backend trait (layout, paint, event) in the stdlib. No backend needs to be implemented yet. Locks in the abstraction boundary early so all higher-level UI work builds against it. Cost: requires a design round before any UI code ships.

options.name: Build one target first, generalize later
options.detail: Pick the most important target (web/WASM), ship it, then extract the abstraction. Faster initial progress but likely forces breaking changes when generalizing. Proven pattern for early-stage projects; risky if the first target's constraints contaminate the API.

options.name: Defer — UI backends post-v1
options.detail: No render-target decision until after v1. Keeps scope tight. Entire reactive-UI stack deferred.
options.code: // No UI framework in Jet v1; users bring their own.

comparisons.note: Defines a thin `RenderObject` seam early; backends (Skia, Impeller, web-canvas) swap beneath it. The seam was designed before all targets existed and held up well.
TUI-only; no backend abstraction. Works for terminals but cannot generalize to GUI without a full rewrite.

decisions.title: Should Jet commit to a layered reactive UI stack as a strategic pillar?
decisions.gist: The proposed stack is: reactivity → view model → typed styles → headless+styled component kit → motion/app kit — each layer building on the previous. This is the TypeScript/Swift UI replacement play. Gated on D-REACTCORE1 (how reactivity works) and D-RENDERTGT1 (backend seam). No layer of this stack should be built until those two gate decisions are made.
decisions.explainer: Committing to this stack means Jet's stdlib eventually includes a full UI framework, not just a signal library. That is a large scope addition — UI frameworks are notoriously hard to get right and to maintain. The payoff is that Jet becomes a genuine TS/Swift alternative for app developers. The risk is years of stdlib work that distracts from language correctness and performance. This decision is about strategic direction, not immediate implementation — no code ships before D-REACTCORE1 and D-RENDERTGT1 are resolved. I8: the stack must have one canonical mechanism at each layer, not multiple competing approaches.
decisions.story: I want to build a web or native app entirely in Jet — not reach for React or SwiftUI. That means Jet needs a first-party UI layer that is reactive, composable, and ships real components.

options.name: Adopt layered stack, sequenced after gate decisions
options.detail: Commit to the strategic direction. Build each layer in order, gated on D-REACTCORE1 + D-RENDERTGT1. No code before those are decided. Long roadmap but gives Jet a genuine app-dev story.

options.name: UI is third-party only
options.detail: Jet ships no UI framework. The signal library (D-REACT1) is the ceiling of stdlib UI support. Third parties build frameworks on top. Keeps stdlib small; risks ecosystem fragmentation (multiple incompatible UI libs).

options.name: Defer — decide at v1
options.detail: No commitment now. Revisit after the language core is stable. Safe for the near term but defers the TS/Swift replacement play indefinitely.
options.code: // No decision — UI story TBD post-v1

comparisons.note: Apple committed to a layered reactive UI stack (Combine → SwiftUI) early. The two-layer seam (reactive model + declarative views) has held up well across platforms.
Elm built the reactive model into the language (The Elm Architecture) and owns the full UI stack. Extremely coherent but brittle to extend beyond its core use-case.
comparisons.code: update Increment model = { model | count = model.count + 1 }

decisions.title: Should Jet model animation/motion as derived reactive state rather than a separate animation runtime?
decisions.gist: The idea: animation is just a time-varying signal — a value that changes over time as derived state in the reactive graph, with no separate animation engine. This is downstream of D-REACTCORE1 (core reactivity) and D-REACTUI1 (stack commitment). Both must be decided first; if either is rejected, this card is moot.
decisions.explainer: If reactivity stays a library (D-REACTCORE1=A) and the UI stack is adopted (D-REACTUI1=A), motion-as-state means the signal library gains a `time` signal and easing/interpolation combinators — animations are just derived signals that read the clock. There is no separate animation runtime to learn. This unifies the mental model but requires the signal library to handle high-frequency updates (60fps+) without excessive re-evaluation overhead. Separate animation runtimes (option B) are usually more efficient but add a second conceptual model. Gated on D-REACTCORE1 and D-REACTUI1.
decisions.story: I want to animate a button press without learning a separate animation API — the button's position should just be a value that smoothly transitions when state changes, using the same signal model I already know.

options.name: Motion = derived signals over time (unified model)
options.detail: The signal library gets a high-frequency `clock` signal and interpolation combinators (spring, tween, ease). Animations are derived signals — no separate API to learn. Requires the runtime to tick signal graphs at frame rate efficiently.

options.name: Separate animation runtime
options.detail: A distinct animation subsystem (timeline, keyframe, physics) runs alongside the reactive graph. More efficient for complex animation workloads but introduces a second conceptual model. Conflicts with I8 (two mechanisms for related jobs).
options.code:
anim.keyframe(target: view.x, to: 100.0, duration: 0.3, curve: .easeOut)
anim.play()

options.name: Defer — decide after D-REACTCORE1 + D-REACTUI1
options.detail: No motion decision until the reactive stack shape is locked. Correct sequencing — this card cannot be usefully decided without those two being resolved first.
options.code: // Block on D-REACTCORE1 and D-REACTUI1 first

comparisons.note: Treats animation as a declarative value (motion values are like signals). Composable and unified with the component model, but still a separate library layer.
comparisons.code:
const x = useMotionValue(0)
const opacity = useTransform(x, [0, 100], [1, 0])

comparisons.note: Animation is driven by state changes, not a separate timeline — close to option A. The reactive model (Combine) and the animation model are unified at the view layer.

decisions.title: Should Jet's runtime adapt behavior to environmental signals (battery, network, load, carbon)?
decisions.gist: The idea is a runtime that reads environmental conditions and adjusts behavior — throttles work on low battery, degrades quality under load, shifts tasks to low-carbon windows. This is a New idea with no existing card. The question is whether this belongs in the language/runtime or in a library that apps call.
decisions.explainer: Environmental adaptation is inherently app-specific policy — what 'degrade under load' means for a video encoder is different from a web server. Baking adaptation into the runtime (option B) risks making the default behavior magical and hard to audit (I1: safe/predictable defaults). A library that exposes signals (battery level, network quality, carbon intensity) and lets app code choose the policy is more composable and auditable. Carbon intensity data requires an external API (electricityMap, WattTime) — the runtime cannot self-contain it. This overlaps with D-ADAPTFID1 (fidelity knob) and D-CARBON1; all three should fold into one decision.
decisions.story: I'm shipping a background sync task. I want it to pause when the battery is below 20%, slow down on metered connections, and prefer running when the grid is clean — without writing platform-specific code for each.

options.name: Library exposing env signals + policy hooks
options.detail: Stdlib exposes a thin `Env` API: battery level, network quality, estimated carbon intensity (via OS/external). App code reads these and sets its own policy. Predictable, auditable, no hidden runtime behavior. Correct match for I1.

options.name: Runtime-managed adaptation
options.detail: The runtime automatically throttles tasks, degrades quality, or defers work based on environmental conditions. Magic and convenient but opaque — hard to debug when behavior differs across devices. Violates predictability (I1 concern).

options.name: Defer / don't add
options.detail: Niche use case. Most apps handle this ad-hoc or via platform APIs. Add only if there is clear demand. Fold the three adaptive cards (runtime, fidelity, carbon) into one decision when the time comes.
options.code: // No stdlib env-adaptation; apps use platform APIs directly

comparisons.note: Constraint-based scheduling (battery, network, idle) as library/framework, not language primitives. Policy is explicit in code.
comparisons.code:
val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
  .setConstraints(Constraints(requiresCharging = true))
  .build()

comparisons.note: OS signals exposed as library APIs; apps poll or observe and apply their own policy. No automatic adaptation.

decisions.title: Should Jet provide a single quality/performance fidelity knob that apps can read and respond to under load?
decisions.gist: A 'fidelity signal' is a single scalar (0.0–1.0) that represents current quality budget. The runtime or platform sets it based on load; app code reads it and degrades gracefully (lower resolution, skip effects, reduce particles). This is a New/library-level idea, closely related to D-ADAPTRT1 (adaptive runtime).
decisions.explainer: This is simpler than D-ADAPTRT1 — rather than a full environmental-signals API, it is one number apps read. The hard question is who sets it: the runtime (automatic, opaque) or the developer explicitly (manual, testable). A library pattern where the fidelity signal is readable and also manually overridable is both useful and auditable. Folding this with D-ADAPTRT1 makes sense — they are the same concept at different granularities. If D-ADAPTRT1 is deferred, defer this too. References: approximate-algorithms and budgets-as-types cards may interact (fidelity budget as a typed value).
decisions.story: My renderer runs at 60fps on a fast machine but stutters on low-end hardware. I want one place in my code to check 'what quality level should I be running at right now' and scale every effect accordingly — without if-else chains spread through every render path.

options.name: Library fidelity signal (read + manual override)
options.detail: Stdlib exposes `Perf.fidelity() -> f32` (set automatically by the runtime based on frame time, or manually by the app for testing). App code reads it and applies its own degradation. Simple, auditable, foldable with D-ADAPTRT1.

options.name: Runtime-managed automatic degradation
options.detail: The runtime detects load and automatically disables features annotated with a fidelity level. App code is unaware of what got disabled. Hard to debug, harder to test.

options.name: Fold into D-ADAPTRT1 / defer
options.detail: Decide this together with the adaptive-runtime card. Not worth a separate ballot slot.
options.code: // Deferred — see D-ADAPTRT1

comparisons.note: Exposes 'scalability groups' (shadow quality, effects quality) as integer levels the engine reads. App code checks `Scalability.GetQualityLevels()`. Explicit, readable, testable.

decisions.title: Should Jet expose carbon-intensity and battery-state signals as stdlib APIs?
decisions.gist: The idea: runtime policies that respond to grid carbon intensity and battery state — pause heavy tasks when carbon is high or battery is low, prefer green windows for scheduled work. This is a New/library-level idea. Carbon intensity requires an external API (not available from the OS). Battery state is OS-provided on most platforms.
decisions.explainer: Battery state is straightforward — every major OS exposes it. Carbon intensity is not: it requires calling an external service (electricityMap, WattTime) or using a locale-derived static estimate. Embedding a live carbon API into stdlib creates an external network dependency inside the language runtime, which is a significant commitment. The simpler approach: expose battery state as a stdlib signal, provide a carbon-intensity hook that apps wire to their preferred data source. This folds cleanly under D-ADAPTRT1. If D-ADAPTRT1 is deferred, defer this too.
decisions.story: I'm running a nightly ML training job. I want it to start only when both the battery is above 80% (or plugged in) and the grid carbon intensity is below a threshold — without writing platform-specific scheduler code.

options.name: Stdlib battery signal + user-provided carbon hook
options.detail: Stdlib provides `Env.battery()` (OS-backed, cross-platform). Carbon intensity is a user-registered hook: app code fetches from its preferred source and registers it. No network dependency inside stdlib. Clean, auditable.

options.name: Full stdlib carbon + battery runtime policies
options.detail: Stdlib bundles a carbon-intensity client (or estimates from locale). Runtime uses both signals to auto-schedule or throttle. Adds external network calls to the language runtime — fragile, hard to test, region-specific accuracy varies wildly.

options.name: Fold into D-ADAPTRT1 / defer
options.detail: Same decision space as adaptive-runtime. Not worth a separate ballot. Decide together.
options.code: // Deferred — see D-ADAPTRT1

comparisons.note: Exposes 'low power mode' and 'battery level' via OS API; scheduler hints (prefersExternalPower) let the OS choose timing. No carbon signal — Apple uses its own internal heuristics.
The standard carbon-intensity data source. Requires API key, network call, locale. Not embeddable in a stdlib without user opt-in.
comparisons.code:
curl 'https://api.electricitymap.org/v3/carbon-intensity/latest?zone=DE' \
  -H 'auth-token: YOUR_TOKEN'

decisions.title: Should jetpack use content-addressed identity for packages and cache entries?
decisions.gist: Content-addressed store: packages are identified by the hash of their content, not just their name+version. Cache entries, build artifacts, and dependency closures are all hash-named. This gives reproducibility, automatic deduplication, and tamper detection. Partially implemented in the build cache; extending it to full package identity (Nix-style) is the question.
decisions.explainer: The current package cache uses hashes for build artifacts but packages are still identified by name+version strings. Full content-addressing means the package store layout changes: packages live at paths like `store/<hash>-name-version/` and two packages with different contents but the same name+version are never confused. This sequences naturally with a signed package cache (D-c56 equivalent) — the signature vouches for a content hash, not a name. Jetpack memory notes the intent. No Nix dependency required — Jet implements its own store. Blast radius: pack.jet format, lock file schema (src/lock.rs), install paths, jetpack CLI output.
decisions.story: I want to pin a dependency to an exact binary — not just a version string that a registry could silently update. And I want two projects that use the same package to share the cached build without re-downloading.
decisions.inWild:
# pack.jet lock entry (content-addressed):
[deps.serde]
version = "1.0.190"
hash = "sha256:3fb9..."
store-path = ".jet/store/3fb9...-serde-1.0.190/"

options.name: Content-addressed package store (extend current cache)
options.detail: Extend the existing build-cache hashing to cover package identity. Lock file records content hash; install path is hash-prefixed. Enables dedup, tamper detection, and a future signed cache. Changes lock file format — requires migration.
options.code:
# .jet/lock (new schema excerpt):
[[package]]
name = "jet-http"
version = "0.3.1"
hash = "sha256:a1b2c3..."
store = ".jet/store/a1b2c3...-jet-http-0.3.1"

# Two projects sharing the same package reuse the same store path.

options.name: Version-named only (status quo)
options.detail: Packages are identified by name+version. Lock file records the version; cache uses version-keyed directories. Simpler but allows silent content drift if a registry republishes a version. No store-layout change needed.
options.code:
# .jet/lock (current schema):
[[package]]
name = "jet-http"
version = "0.3.1"
# No hash — version is the identity

options.name: Hash lock file only (no store-path change)
options.detail: Record a content hash in the lock file for tamper detection, but keep the store layout version-named. Adds integrity checking without changing install paths. Middle ground — less dedup benefit but lower migration cost.
options.code:
# .jet/lock (hybrid):
[[package]]
name = "jet-http"
version = "0.3.1"
hash = "sha256:a1b2c3..."  # verified on install, store path unchanged

comparisons.note: Full content-addressed store — every package path includes the hash of its inputs. Zero silent drift, perfect dedup. High implementation complexity but proven at scale.
comparisons.code: /nix/store/a1b2c3...-curl-7.88.1/bin/curl

comparisons.note: Lock file records content hash (Cargo.lock `checksum`) but store layout is version-named. Option C is what Cargo does — integrity checking without full content-addressing.
comparisons.code:
# Cargo.lock:
[[package]]
name = "serde"
version = "1.0.190"
source = "registry+https://github.com/rust-lang/crates.io-index"
checksum = "9c4f1..."

decisions.comment: I already ratified a different structure for the install path though, <name>-<version>-<hash>, not has prefix. Ensure we use mine

decisions.title: Reopen procedural macros / arbitrary AST injection for Jet?
decisions.gist: D-METADEPTH1 and D-CTCODEGEN1 rejected user-defined AST rewriting for v1. The question is whether to revisit that rejection — either now, gated, or as a post-self-host research track. Current coverage comes from `#[derive]`, reflection, and `$splice` inside `comptime {}` blocks.
decisions.explainer: Proc macros let user code transform the AST of arbitrary other code before semantic analysis. They were rejected because they create an unbounded second surface of syntax and type rules that the front end no longer fully owns — violating I8 (one canonical mechanism) and making tooling (the LSP, diagnostics) unreliable. The safe cases are covered by `#[derive]` for structural code generation and `$splice` for comptime value injection. Reopening requires revisiting D-METADEPTH1 and D-CTCODEGEN1. Any gated form would interact with the user-derives card and the full-jai-metaprogramming track (c154).
decisions.story: I want to write a library that generates a state machine from an annotated enum without forking the compiler — right now I have to hand-write the expansion or wait for an official derive.

options.name: Keep rejected for v1
options.detail: Derives, reflection, and `$splice` cover the safe-structural cases. Full proc macros give arbitrary user code control over the AST before sema, which breaks I8 (a new syntax surface per macro) and I2/I3 (sema can no longer own all checking). No new action needed.

options.name: Allow gated proc macros (opt-in, audited)
options.detail: A library marks a function `@proc_macro` and it receives an AST token tree, transforming it before sema. Gated behind `#[Grant(ProcMacro)]` at the call site so readers see the risk. Still violates I8 — it is a second expansion surface running before the canonical checker.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-self-host research
options.detail: Park the idea as a research item under the full-jai-metaprogramming track (c154). Revisit only after Jet is self-hosted and the AST/sema boundary is stable enough to define a safe proc-macro API. No current action; decision stays rejected.

comparisons.note: Proc macros operate on raw `TokenStream` before type checking. They can produce invalid code that causes cryptic rustc errors, and IDEs struggle to provide completions inside macro-generated spans.
Zig has no proc macros; comptime functions operate on fully-typed values. This is closer to Jet's `$splice` model — safe, checkable, no separate AST surface.

decisions.title: Reopen library-defined sigils, keywords, or grammar (reader macros) for Jet?
decisions.gist: D-EXT1 classified grammar mutation (Tier 4 extensions) as a global footgun and rejected it. Reader macros let libraries introduce new sigils, keywords, or syntax rules. The question is whether any sandboxed form is worth reopening, or whether the rejection stands.
decisions.explainer: Reader macros change the tokenizer or parser table for the duration of a module or file. They violate I7 (every user-typeable sigil lives in Source/Syntax.rs with a decision ID) and I8 (grammar becomes per-library, not one surface). Tooling — the LSP, formatter, syntax highlighter — cannot reason about code it has not seen the grammar for. Even a sandboxed form requires the parser to be extensible, which is a major architectural commitment. Marked DSL blocks (`#[Sql] { ... }`) are the stdlib-only safety valve already ratified under D-EXT1. No new prerequisites exist for a gated form.
decisions.story: I want to write a parsing library that introduces `<< >>` as stream operators without waiting for a language proposal — like Haskell's `do` notation or Raku's grammar system.

options.name: Keep rejected — grammar is fixed
options.detail: I7 requires every sigil in Source/Syntax.rs. Reader macros would mean any library could silently redefine what `<<` or `>>` mean in a file. DSL blocks handle the common case; new operators go through the ballot process. Strong recommendation.
options.code:
// Error if user lib tries to add a sigil:
error[E0900]: unknown sigil `<<` in expression
  --> src/stream.jet:4:12
   |
 4 |   let x = buf << 16;
   |              ^^ not a defined operator
   |   hint: define operators via the ballot process, not reader macros

options.name: Allow grammar extensions in an isolated scope
options.detail: A `#[Grammar(ext)]` block opts a file into a named grammar extension published as a package. The parser downloads and applies the extension grammar. This is sandboxed per-file but breaks the LSP, formatter, and any tool that assumes a fixed grammar. Violates I7/I8.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-v1 grammar versioning research
options.detail: Park as research under a grammar-versioning track. Before any extension mechanism, Jet would need content-addressed grammar snapshots and tooling APIs for grammar consumers. Not actionable now; rejection stands.

comparisons.note: Reader macros dispatch on arbitrary characters before tokenization. They are expressive but mean any Lisp file's syntax can be completely foreign to a reader who does not know its reader macro set.
Grammars are first-class and composable, making Raku highly expressive — and nearly unreadable across different grammar extensions in practice.

decisions.title: Add a full logic-programming subset (backtracking, multi-answer relations) to Jet?
decisions.gist: Research notes caution against a full logic-programming subset. The gentler slice — failure-aware iterators and comprehensions — is already on the roadmap. The question is whether to add true multi-answer relations and backtracking on top of that, or hold the line.
decisions.explainer: Full LP (Prolog-style) requires unification, a choice-point stack, and a non-deterministic execution model that cuts across Jet's deterministic ownership semantics. It would introduce a second execution model with different rules for variable binding, mutation, and resource cleanup — directly conflicting with I8 and with the safety-by-default guarantee. The failure-aware-comprehension card covers the practical 90% case (generators that can fail or produce multiple results) without a separate execution model. A full LP subsystem would also complicate the JIT tier and codegen.
decisions.story: I want to write a solver that enumerates valid configurations of a constraint system — like a puzzle solver or a type-inference engine — without shelling out to Prolog.

options.name: Reject full LP — keep failure-aware iterators only
options.detail: The failure-aware-comprehension card already targets the practical use cases. Full backtracking introduces a second execution model (choice points, unification) incompatible with deterministic ownership. Recommend keeping the door closed.

options.name: Adopt a scoped LP subset (relations block)
options.detail: A `@logic { }` block opts in to a Datalog-style subset: finite relations, no function symbols, stratified negation. Bounded and terminating, so no infinite search trees. Still a second execution model — variables inside the block bind differently — which violates I8.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-v1 constraint/solver research
options.detail: Park LP as a research item. A future constraint-programming library (not a language feature) could implement backtracking via a continuation monad or explicit search stack, keeping the language surface clean. No language change needed.

comparisons.note: Full LP with backtracking and unification. Powerful for combinatorial search but the non-deterministic execution model is notoriously hard to reason about for programmers from imperative backgrounds.
comparisons.code:
path(X, Z) :- edge(X, Y), path(Y, Z).
?- path(1, Z).
Z = 2 ;
Z = 3.

comparisons.note: A minimal logic DSL embedded in a host language. It works but requires the programmer to think in a completely different evaluation model — the very friction Jet wants to avoid.
comparisons.code:
(run* (q)
  (fresh (x y)
    (== q (list x y))
    (membero x '(1 2))
    (membero y '(a b))))

decisions.title: Commit to a structural (AST/semantic) merge tool for Jet version control?
decisions.gist: Structural merge resolves version-control conflicts using the program's AST or semantic identity rather than line-based text diff. This is new and not yet carded for implementation. It depends on content-addressed definitions and a semantic index, neither of which is built.
decisions.explainer: Line-based merge fails when two branches rename a function, reorder arguments, or extract a helper — producing conflicts that are trivially safe or spurious conflicts that obscure real ones. A structural merge tool would compare AST nodes by identity (name + signature or content address), resolve renames and moves automatically, and surface only semantic conflicts. Prerequisites: stable AST serialization, content-addressed definitions (its own unbuilt card), and a semantic index API. This is a tooling feature, not a language feature — it does not touch syntax or sema, so I1/I8 are not at risk. But it is a large, standalone project that competes for capacity with in-flight compiler work.
decisions.story: I refactored a module across two branches — one renamed a function, the other added parameters. Git thinks it's a conflict. A structural merge tool would see they touched different things and merge cleanly.

options.name: Far-horizon: capture, don't build now
options.detail: Record the idea and its prerequisites (content-addressed defs, semantic index). Build neither until those foundations exist. The semantic index and content-addressed-definitions cards must land first; revisit structural merge after they do. No current action.

options.name: Build a structural merge tool now
options.detail: Start the tool alongside the compiler. Requires inventing an AST serialization format and a merge algorithm before the AST is stable. High risk of rework as the language evolves. Not recommended.

options.name: Reject — out of scope
options.detail: Structural merge is a tooling feature orthogonal to the language. Jet can ship v1 without it; existing Git workflows are sufficient. The effort is better spent on the compiler. Reject and don't revisit.
options.code:
// No action. Developers use standard git merge.
// Conflict resolution is a developer workflow problem, not a language problem.

comparisons.note: A structural diff tool using tree-sitter grammars. Shows diffs in terms of AST nodes rather than lines. Does not do merging — only diffing — but demonstrates the value of structural comparison.
comparisons.code:
# difftastic output (not Jet):
# left.py            right.py
# def foo(x):        def foo(x, y):  # added param
#     return x + 1       return x + y

comparisons.note: GitHub's experimental semantic merge tool parsed code into typed syntax trees and merged on AST identity. Abandoned in 2021 — the project underestimated the complexity of a language-agnostic merge algorithm.
comparisons.code:
# github/semantic (archived)
# semantic diff --language python a.py b.py
# → proved the concept; proved it was hard to generalize

decisions.title: Treat 'structural merge by meaning' as a distinct card, or fold into D-STRUCTMERGE1?
decisions.gist: This card and the structural-merge card (D-STRUCTMERGE1) describe the same idea from two angles: merging by AST identity vs. merging by program meaning/semantics. Keeping two cards creates duplicate tracking and splits owner attention on what is effectively one research item.
decisions.explainer: D-STRUCTMERGE1 captures AST/semantic structural merge. This card adds the 'meaning' framing — understanding whether two edits are semantically equivalent even if textually different. In practice, any structural merge tool would need to handle both: identity-based merge for renames/moves, and meaning-based equivalence for refactors. They are not independent research tracks. Consolidating them into one card (D-STRUCTMERGE1) eliminates the I8 violation of two mechanisms for one job and keeps the owner's ballot queue shorter. The distinction between 'identity' and 'meaning' is an implementation detail of the one tool, not a reason for two cards.
decisions.story: I don't want to review two separate ballot cards for what is clearly the same future tooling feature — one entry on the research backlog is enough.

options.name: Fold into D-STRUCTMERGE1 (consolidate)
options.detail: Close this card. Add a note to D-STRUCTMERGE1 that 'meaning-based equivalence' is part of the same research track. One far-horizon item, one owner decision, no duplicate ballot entries. Directly respects I8 at the process level.

options.name: Keep as a distinct card
options.detail: Argue that 'merge by identity' (rename detection) and 'merge by meaning' (semantic equivalence) are distinct research problems that may require different tools and timelines. Track separately. Creates two far-horizon items where one would do.

comparisons.note: Most issue trackers close duplicate cards with a 'duplicate of #N' tag. The standard practice is to consolidate and add notes to the canonical card rather than run parallel tracks for the same research question.
comparisons.code:
# CLOSED as duplicate of D-STRUCTMERGE1
# Added to D-STRUCTMERGE1 scope:
#   - meaning/semantic equivalence detection
#   - not just AST identity

decisions.title: How is a whole-graph effect PROHIBITION spelled on a function signature?
decisions.gist: D-PROP1=A ratified that a function can forbid one effect across its entire reachable call graph, on the same propagation engine as the positive `#(Net)` effect set. This decides only how that prohibition reads. It must not collide with the positive effect-set syntax already in `#(...)`.
decisions.explainer:
The positive surface is the effect set `#(Net, Io)` (D-EFF1/D-QUAL1). A prohibition is the inverse walk: it names one effect the function and every reachable callee may NOT use. Purely surface; no new engine machinery (I3 holds, erased in codegen). Blast radius: parser marker/effect-tag grammar + Syntax.rs.

Recommendation: A — `!` is the universal 'not' sigil, keeps both polarities in one readable set, reuses `#(...)` with no new marker.

options.label: Negation inside the effect set: `#(!Net)`
options.body:
`!` before an effect name inside `#(...)` flips 'may use' to 'must never reach'; polarities coexist.
```jet
#(Io, !Net) fn audit_log(event: Event) { write_local(event) }
```
One surface for both polarities; one place to read the function's effect rules.

options.label: Dedicated marker: `#Forbid(Net)`
options.body:
A standalone PascalCase marker carries the banned effect.
```jet
#Forbid(Net)
#(Io) fn audit_log(event: Event) { write_local(event) }
```
Reads as a loud separate rule; matches the argument-marker family (`#Grant(Fs)`). Cost: a second surface to read.

options.label: Sign prefix inside the set: `#(-Net)`
options.body:
`-` before an effect name marks it forbidden.
```jet
#(Io, -Net) fn audit_log(event: Event) { write_local(event) }
```
Compact like A, but `-` reads as set-subtraction and misreads more easily than `!`.

decisions.title: What surface declares a request/response protocol, and how is a generated handle used?
decisions.gist: D-PROTO1=A ratified that the compiler generates ordered Client/Server handle types over linear (`#SingleUse`) + typestate (`state`/`#Transition`). This decides the declaration spelling. The exchange should read top-to-bottom as a sequence — that readability is the point.
decisions.explainer:
D-LIN1 and D-STATE1 are ratified; this is the declaration surface + the handle threaded. Blast radius: a new top-level construct in the parser + Syntax.rs and codegen lowering to linear+typestate. I8: one canonical mechanism for ordered protocols.

Recommendation: A — `protocol` is the plain word a beginner reads right, keeps the exchange in one block, generates both sides as D-PROTO1=A requires.

options.label: `protocol Name { ... }` block of ordered messages
options.body:
A `protocol` block names each `client -> server` step; compiler emits `Name.Client`/`Name.Server` handles.
```jet
protocol Handshake {
  client -> server: Hello(version: Int)
  server -> client: Ack(session: Id)
  client -> server: Bye
}
fn drive(h: Handshake.Client) {
  c@ Handshake.Client = h.Hello(3)
  c2@ .. = c.recv_Ack()
  c2.Bye()
}
```
Sequence reads in one place; both sides from one declaration; out-of-order = type error.

options.label: `session Name { ... }` keyword
options.body:
Same structure, the session-types term.
```jet
session Handshake { client -> server: Hello(version: Int) }
```
Precise for experts; but `session` is jargon and collides with login-session meaning.

options.label: Reuse `state`+`#Transition` by hand (no new keyword)
options.body:
User writes a `#SingleUse` handle + hand-annotates `#Transition`; session-ness derived.
Maximum reuse, zero keyword — but the user hand-writes both sides and keeps them dual, the boilerplate a protocol declaration exists to erase (D-PROTO1's rejected B).

decisions.title: Does `|` bind tighter than `||`/`&&` in match arms, and are parens required or cosmetic?
decisions.gist: D-MATCHARM1=A ratified the split: `|` alternates values, `||`/`&&` combine with booleans, parens group. This decides precedence between `|` and `||`/`&&`, and whether parens are load-bearing or cosmetic. It changes how an unparenthesized head parses.
decisions.explainer:
For `400 | 404 && fresh`: if `|` binds tighter it reads `(400|404) && fresh`; if `&&` binds tighter, `400 | (404 && fresh)`. Blast radius: parser arm-head precedence + the D-PAT `&&` guard rule (confirm the two `&&` unify). Beginner note: a silently-misread head is a footgun.

Recommendation: B — Beginner-first: a mixed head can be silently misread, so forcing parens there removes the footgun while simple heads stay clean.

options.label: `|` tighter; parens optional (cosmetic)
options.body:
`|` tightest, then `&&`, then `||` (C-family). Parens only override.
```jet
400 | 404 && fresh -> retry   // (400|404) && fresh
500 | 501 || n==0 -> abort    // (500|501) || (n==0)
```
Familiar, fewest keystrokes — but a reader must know the table.

options.label: `|` tighter; parens REQUIRED on a mixed head
options.body:
Same precedence, but mixing `|` with `||`/`&&` demands explicit parens (teaching error otherwise).
```jet
400 | 404 -> ok                 // fine
(400 | 404) && fresh -> retry   // required
400 | 404 && fresh -> // ERROR: group with parens
```
No silent misread; costs parens on rare mixed arms. Most beginner-safe.

options.label: Flat left-to-right; parens the only grouping
options.body:
No precedence; strictly L-to-R, parens the sole grouping.
Simplest rule to state, but L-to-R surprises anyone expecting `&&` over `||` and still allows confusing mixes.

decisions.title: What is the visible discard sigil for a `#MustUse` / `T ? E` result?
decisions.gist: D-IGNORERET1=B ratified that discarding a fallible result must be explicit + visible (never silent, I1) and emits a lint pointing at what was dropped. This decides the spelling. It must be impossible to type by accident and obvious in review.
decisions.explainer:
`#MustUse` makes ignoring a fallible result a compile error; this is the one sanctioned escape. Blast radius: parser, the `#MustUse` sema check (error→lint when present), a W-code + ui snapshot. The sigil must not resemble normal binding.

Recommendation: A — `!_` is postfix like `?`, visually unmistakable, and the `!` signals deliberate intent — impossible to type by reflex unlike `_ =`.

options.label: Trailing `!_`
options.body:
Postfix `!_` discards loudly; `!` reads as 'on purpose'.
```jet
write_log(event)!_   // lints: dropped `Io ? IoError`
```
Distinct from everything else, postfix like `?`, flags intent. Cannot be typed by reflex.

options.label: Word form `!discard`
options.body:
Postfix keyword spells intent.
```jet
write_log(event) !discard
```
Most self-documenting; heavier, and a keyword for a rare op.

options.label: Leading `_ = expr`
options.body:
Bind to throwaway, Go/Rust style.
```jet
_ = write_log(event)
```
Familiar — but reads as ordinary assignment, the reflexive habit that makes silent-drop easy; understates deliberateness.

decisions.title: How does interpolation select the Debug hook instead of the default Display hook?
decisions.gist: D-DISPLAYDBG1=A ratified two hooks — Display (default) and Debug (auto-derived). This decides the interpolation spelling that switches a `{x}` slot to Debug. It rides on the ratified `{...}` interpolation surface (S8).
decisions.explainer:
S8 is `"hi {name}"`, rendering via Display. This adds a per-slot Debug selector. Blast radius: the in-string interpolation parser, the formatter (must round-trip the selector — formatter-round-trip rule), codegen dispatch. I8: one selector for one job, not a format mini-language.

Recommendation: A — `{x:?}` is the established unambiguous convention many users know, and can't be mistaken for a real member access like `.debug`.

options.label: Rust-style `{x:?}`
Method-ish `{user.debug}`
options.body:
Append `.debug` to the slot.
```jet
print("{user} vs {user.debug}")
```
Reads in plain Jet, no new punctuation. Cost: looks like a real member (collides if a type has `debug`).

options.label: Bang selector `{user!}`
options.body:
Trailing `!` picks Debug — 'show me everything'.
```jet
print("{user} vs {user!}")
```
Shortest; `!` already reads 'raw' in Jet. Cost: `!` overloaded, easy to miss in a long string.

decisions.title: What is the marker name for the replay-soundness function marker?
decisions.gist: D-REPLAY1=A ratified a function marker that rejects any reachable un-mockable `#(Time/Rand/Net/Io)` via inverse propagation. This is a low-stakes rubber-stamp of the NAME, matching the `#Pure`/`#Test` convention.
decisions.explainer:
Pure naming; no semantics at stake. PascalCase `#`-marker (D-CASING1) on a function. Blast radius: Syntax.rs keyword, parser, one ui snapshot, examples.

Recommendation: A — `#Replayable` matches the property-reading marker family and states what the guarantee buys without over-claiming.

options.label: `#Replayable`
options.body:
Names the guarantee.
```jet
#Replayable fn settle(order: Order, clock: Clock) -> Receipt { ... }
```
Matches the `-able` 'property of this fn' convention; says exactly what it buys.

options.label: `#Deterministic`
options.body:
Names the underlying property.
```jet
#Deterministic fn settle(...) -> Receipt { ... }
```
Accurate but over-claims (effect-free ≠ fully deterministic) and is longer/more abstract.

options.label: `#Replay`
options.body:
Bare noun.
```jet
#Replay fn settle(...) -> Receipt { ... }
```
Terse, but reads as a command/mode, not a property the fn HAS.

decisions.title: Which backing implementation powers the opt-in `Gc<T>` traced handle? (I6 owner gate)
decisions.gist: D-OPTGC1=A ratified `Gc<T>` as a library-only opt-in traced handle (ownership stays default). This is an I6 external-dependency approval gate: the collector either needs an owner-approved crate or a hand-rolled stdlib implementation. Per I6 any external dep is runtime-side only, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation.
decisions.explainer:
`Gc<T>` is an expert opt-in (I1: never the default). The collector is real machinery — mark/sweep with a root set + tracing. I6 governs the backing exactly like Cranelift/regex/wasmtime. Blast radius: a stdlib module + `.jet/lock` pin if a crate is approved. Does not touch `Source/`.

Recommendation: A — A pure-Rust stdlib mark-sweep is the I6 end-state with zero gated dep and no native-ize debt; effort is never a deterrent.

options.label: Hand-roll pure-Rust mark-sweep in stdlib (no external dep)
options.body:
A small tracing mark-sweep in stdlib, std-only, no crate.
```jet
import mem.gc
node@ Gc<Node> = gc.alloc(Node.{ value: 1, next: none })
```
I6: nothing to native-ize — this IS the end-state; no gated dep, no lock pin. Most up-front work, which philosophy says is not a deterrent.

options.label: Adopt a pure-Rust GC crate (e.g. `gc`/`broom`) runtime-side
options.body:
Vetted pure-Rust tracing-GC crate as a runtime-side bootstrap, gated like Cranelift.
I6: owner-gated, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation to replace by Epoch-3. Faster to a working `Gc<T>` but adds a dep we must remove.

options.label: Defer until a concrete use-case
options.body:
Keep `Gc<T>` reserved/unimplemented with a 'no GC backend yet' diagnostic until a real program needs it.
No dep/code now; cost: leaves a ratified feature a stub when the use-case (cyclic graphs) is already known.

decisions.title: Which crypto primitive backend powers `crypto.seal/open` + `sign/verify`? (I6 owner gate)
decisions.gist: D-CRYPTOENV1=A ratified the seal/open + sign/verify envelope. This is an I6 external-dependency approval gate for the underlying AEAD/signature primitives. Pure-Rust is preferred for the native-ize end-state.
decisions.explainer:
Hand-rolling primitive crypto is a footgun (constant-time, audited impls). A vetted backend is required; I6 governs which: runtime-side only, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Differentiator is the backend's I6 posture. Blast radius: a stdlib `crypto` module + `.jet/lock` pin.

Recommendation: A — RustCrypto is pure Rust with no C/asm, the closest of the three to the I6 end-state and simplest to re-implement first-party.

options.label: Pure-Rust RustCrypto (aes-gcm/chacha20poly1305/ed25519-dalek)
options.body:
Audited pure-Rust crates, gated runtime-side like Cranelift.
```jet
import crypto
box@ Bytes = crypto.seal(key, plaintext)?
sig@ Bytes = crypto.sign(privkey, msg)
crypto.verify(pubkey, msg, sig)?
```
I6: pure Rust, no C/asm — closest to the native-ize end-state, easiest to re-implement first-party.

options.label: `ring` (C/asm, BoringSSL-derived)
options.body:
Battle-tested, fast.
I6: pulls in C + assembly, needs a C toolchain, pins a non-Rust core — furthest from the end-state.

options.label: libsodium via FFI
options.body:
Bind system libsodium through the stdlib FFI-bridge pattern.
Widely audited, misuse-resistant — but an external C library + system dep (nixpkgs-interim), heaviest to native-ize, worst non-Nix story.

decisions.title: Should the leading enum-variant dot also apply in value position when the expected type is known?
decisions.gist: D-ENUMDOT1=A ratified the leading dot on enum-variant patterns in match arms (`.Circle(r)`). This decides whether that dot extends to VALUE position when the expected type is known (`c@ Color = .Red` alongside `Color.Red`). A coherent but separate extension the owner flagged for an explicit ruling.
decisions.explainer:
Today value-position is `Color.Red` (S30); the dot was added only to match arms (S31). Extending it mirrors dot-construction (`.{ }`, D-DOTCTOR) — type-directed authoring (Blueprint north-star). The dot resolves only where the expected type is known (annotated binding, return, typed arg). Blast radius: parser expression grammar, expected-type elaboration, every enum literal in canon/examples.

Recommendation: A — Extending the dot mirrors dot-construction and the owner's type-directed anti-repetition direction, while keeping `Color.Red` where no expected type exists.

options.label: Extend the dot to value position (both spellings)
options.body:
`.Red` allowed anywhere the expected type is known; `Color.Red` stays valid everywhere.
```jet
c@ Color = .Red
fn default() -> Color { .Red }
paint(.Red)
x@ = Color.Red   // no expected type -> qualified form
```
Mirrors dot-construction and the match-arm dot; type-directed, less repetition. Rule: 'use the dot when the type is known.'

options.label: Keep the dot match-arm-only
options.body:
Value position stays `Color.Red`.
```jet
c@ Color = Color.Red
match shape { .Circle(r) -> ... }
```
Smallest surface, no new ambiguity — but the dot means 'inferred member' in patterns yet is absent in the symmetric value case.

options.label: Require the dot everywhere; retire `Color.Red`
options.body:
`.Red` the single spelling where the type is known; drop `Color.Red`.
One canonical spelling (I8-pure) but breaks the no-expected-type case and churns every `Type.Variant` literal.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue refinement types (e.g. PositiveInt proved > 0), and if so as a construction-time subset or a full SMT-backed prover?
decisions.gist: We're deciding whether Jet should let you attach a predicate to a type — PositiveInt = Int where it > 0 — so the value is known good everywhere it flows, instead of re-checking with scattered require() calls. The real fork is how much proving the compiler does: nothing (decline), a pragmatic subset proved at construction plus flow-narrowing (no theorem prover), or a full SMT-solver-backed prover. The central cost of the full version is that an SMT solver is a large external dependency, which collides head-on with I6 (zero external crates in the compiler).
decisions.explainer: A refinement type is a base type plus a predicate the compiler tracks as part of the type: once a value has type PositiveInt, no callee needs to re-validate it. The win is real — it removes a class of beginner footguns (forgot to check) and a class of expert boilerplate (re-checking the same invariant at every layer). The danger is duplicating I8: Jet already has require()/T ? E/? for runtime validation, so refinement types must extend that path, not fork it — construction must funnel through one fallible smart-constructor that returns PositiveInt ? Error, reusing require under the hood. The deep divide is foundational-vs-research. A subset that only proves predicates at the construction boundary (literal-checked, or returned as T ? E) and then narrows them flow-sensitively (after if x > 0, x is PositiveInt in that branch) needs no solver — it's a few sema rules over existing machinery and could land in Epoch 3. The full version — proving that arbitrary arithmetic preserves a predicate, e.g. that a+b stays in-range — needs a decision procedure, i.e. an SMT solver (Z3-class). That is the I6 problem: it's tens of thousands of lines of external C++/Rust we cannot vendor under our zero-external-crate rule, it makes errors come from a solver (risking I2: rustc/solver must never speak to users), and solver timeouts make compile times nondeterministic. So the honest framing is: the cheap, safe, beginner-friendly slice (B) is mostly independent of the expensive research slice (C), and we can ship the former without ever committing to the latter.
decisions.story: I'm writing a billing function and I type fn charge(cents: PositiveInt). A caller passes a value computed from user input. The compiler stops me at the call site: it can't prove the value is positive, and it points me at the one constructor — PositiveInt.new(n) returns PositiveInt ? String — so I write let amt = PositiveInt.new(raw)? once at the boundary. From there it flows through three layers of my code untouched, and nobody re-checks it. When I later guard with if amt > 0 the compiler already knew; when I forgot a guard last week, require() would have blown up at runtime — now it's a compile error with a fix-it pointing at the constructor.

options.name: Decline — keep refinement types out of scope
options.detail: Do not add refinement types at all. Keep validation on the existing require()/T ? E/? path: callers validate at boundaries and pass plain Int. Honest rationale: this is the smallest surface, fully I6/I8-clean, and beginners already get safe-by-default behavior because forgetting a require() fails loudly at runtime (exit 70) rather than silently corrupting. The cost is the duplicated-invariant smell — the same predicate gets re-checked at multiple layers, and the type system can't prove a value stays good as it flows. Recommended only if we judge the subset's ongoing sema/formatter/diagnostic maintenance not worth the boilerplate it removes. Not recommended: it leaves a real beginner footgun (a forgotten check is a runtime crash, not a compile error) that B fixes cheaply.

options.name: Pragmatic subset — construction-checked predicate types + flow narrowing, NO solver
options.detail: RECOMMENDED. Add `refine T = Base where <predicate>;`. The predicate is checked at exactly one place — the generated `.new` smart constructor returns `T ? Error`, lowering to the existing require()/T ? E machinery (no new error path → I8 respected). Once you hold a `T`, every callee trusts it; passing a bare `Base` where `T` is expected is a compile error pointing at `.new`. Add flow-sensitive narrowing: inside `if x > 0 { … }` a plain Int narrows to PositiveInt for that branch, and literal arguments (`charge(5)`) are checked at compile time. Crucially NO general theorem proving: the compiler does NOT try to prove `a + b` stays positive — arithmetic on refined values widens back to the base type, and you re-establish the refinement through `.new` at the next boundary. This is a handful of sema rules over machinery Jet already has; realistically lands in Epoch 3. Gives beginners a compile-time guarantee (forgot-the-check becomes a type error) and experts a way to encode invariants once, without an SMT dependency. The deliberate limitation (arithmetic widens) is the honest seam that keeps us out of solver territory.

options.name: Full SMT-backed refinement types (post-Epoch research)
options.detail: Liquid-Haskell/F*/Dafny-class: the compiler proves that operations PRESERVE predicates — that `a + b` is positive, that an index stays in bounds, that a returned value satisfies its refinement for all inputs — by discharging verification conditions to an SMT solver. This is the strongest guarantee (eliminates whole classes of runtime checks and is genuinely magic). It is also the expensive, risky path and is NOT recommended for now. Central cost is I6: an SMT solver (Z3-class) is tens of thousands of lines of external C++/Rust we cannot vendor under zero-external-crate; writing our own decision procedure is a multi-year research project of its own. Secondary costs: solver output must never reach users (I2) so we'd need to translate every failed proof into a Jet diagnostic; solver timeouts make compile times nondeterministic (anti-beginner); and the annotation burden (writing predicates the solver can discharge) is an expert-only skill that conflicts with beginner-magic defaults. Reasonable as a FUTURE research track layered on top of B's surface syntax — B's `refine` definitions become the predicates C would later prove — but committing now means owning the I6 carve-out and the solver-error translation problem. Treat as research, gated behind its own decision when/if a pure-Jet decision procedure exists.

comparisons.note: Bolts refinement types onto GHC and discharges proof obligations to an external SMT solver (Z3). Predicates are written in special comments; the solver proves arithmetic/measure facts. Exactly the model option C describes — and exactly the external-solver dependency I6 forbids us from vendoring.

subtype PositiveInt is Integer with Dynamic_Predicate => PositiveInt > 0. Plain Ada checks the predicate at construction/assignment AT RUNTIME (raises Constraint_Error) — this is essentially option B's construction-time model. SPARK then adds an optional separate prover pass to discharge them statically (option C). The Ada/SPARK split is the clean precedent for shipping B first and treating C as a layered, optional research tier.

No real refinements; simulates them with a phantom 'brand' and a user-written guard that asserts the brand. The type only means anything because one constructor is the sole place that mints it. This is a no-solver pattern very close to option B's smart-constructor discipline — proof its construction-time core is viable without any prover.

Has no refinement types at all; the idiom is exactly Jet's status quo — a newtype wrapping a fallible constructor (NonZeroU32::new returns Option). The ecosystem reaching for newtype+constructor (and never getting compiler-proved arithmetic) shows option A is a coherent, shippable resting point, and that B is the natural, low-cost step beyond it.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue machine-checked formal verification, and if so as a bounded foundational checker, a full proof-carrying-code engine, or not at all?
decisions.gist: A request to attach machine-checked proofs to functions (e.g. prove constant_time_eq is input-independent) and refuse to ship if the proof fails. Real proof engines (SMT solvers, theorem provers) are enormous external dependencies that collide head-on with I6 (zero external crates in the compiler). The question is whether any verification story belongs in Jet, and if so, the narrowest honest form.
decisions.explainer: Formal verification spans a huge cost gradient. At the cheap end, bounded/exhaustive checking and property-tests-as-contracts give real machine-checked guarantees for small finite domains with zero new dependencies — we already own the test runner and comptime evaluator. At the expensive end, a true proof of a universally-quantified property over an infinite domain needs an SMT solver (Z3 is ~500k lines of C++) or a proof assistant (Lean/Coq), each a massive external dependency that violates I6 in the one place I6 is strictest: the compiler itself. The honest tradeoff: anything that proves 'for all inputs' either ships a solver in the default path (no), gates one behind an opt-in expert wall that is never reached by beginners and never required to build (maybe, Epoch 3+), or stays research (post-Epoch). It matters because verification is the master-of-ALL pitch for crypto/safety-critical code, but a second checking mechanism risks I8 (we already have #Test) and a solver in the build risks I2/I6. The pragmatic subset must be a deepening of #Test, not a rival to it.
decisions.story: I'm writing a constant-time comparison for a password check. I write the function, mark it #Verify(constant_time), and `jet build` either proves the timing is input-independent and ships, or refuses with a diagnostic pointing at the branch that leaks. I never install a solver, never learn Dafny, and a teammate who's never heard of formal methods can read the marker and know exactly what's guaranteed. The day my logic stops being checkable by the bounded checker, Jet tells me plainly instead of silently downgrading to 'probably fine'.

options.name: Decline — testing + property testing + the #Unsafe audit story is the sanctioned path
options.detail: Jet does not pursue machine-checked proofs. The existing mechanisms cover the real need: #Test blocks for examples, property-style #Test with generated inputs for invariants, and #Unsafe("reason") audited regions for code that needs expert-grade scrutiny. Verification of 'for all inputs' is declined as out of scope: it cannot be done honestly without an external solver (I6 violation in the compiler) and risks a second checking mechanism (I8). A function like constant_time_eq is handled by an audited #Unsafe region plus property tests, with the audit reason documenting the human-reviewed timing argument. This keeps the default surface tiny, the build dependency-free, and the beginner story unchanged. Cost: Jet can never *prove* a property; crypto/safety-critical users who want machine-checked guarantees reach for SPARK/Dafny/F* and FFI the result in.

options.name: Bounded foundational checker — #Verify as an exhaustive/randomized contract, deepening #Test (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship #Verify(<predicate>) as a compile-time contract evaluated by Jet's OWN comptime engine and test runner — never an external solver, never in the default beginner path, and an opt-in marker on the functions that want it. Semantics: for a forall over a small finite domain (e.g. U8 x U8), the checker enumerates EXHAUSTIVELY at build time and the property is genuinely machine-checked for that domain. For domains too large to enumerate, it falls back to randomized + boundary sampling and the diagnostic states plainly 'checked by sampling, not proven' so the guarantee is never oversold. #Verify is one mechanism with #Test (I8 held): #Test = 'these concrete cases pass'; #Verify = 'this quantified predicate holds over its (bounded) domain' — a strict generalization run by the same engine, not a rival. A failed #Verify is a build error (T ? VerifyError surfaces the witness). Zero new compiler dependencies (I6 held). Honest ceiling: it cannot prove anything over an infinite domain — that's explicitly Option C's job and #Verify says so when it samples.

options.name: Full proof-carrying code — #Prove backed by an external SMT/proof engine behind an expert opt-in (post-Epoch research)
options.detail: The literal ask: machine-checked proofs of universally-quantified properties over infinite domains (true constant-time, no-overflow-ever, functional correctness vs a spec). This requires a real proof backend — an SMT solver (Z3) or a proof assistant (Lean/Coq/Why3) — which is an enormous external dependency. It is admitted ONLY behind an #Unsafe-grade expert gate that (1) is never on the default build path, (2) is never required to compile any program, (3) is opt-in per-project and per-function via #Prove, and (4) is wired as an FFI/bridge backend (per the FFI-bridge stdlib pattern) so the solver is invoked as an external tool, never linked into the Source/ compiler — keeping I6 intact for the compiler proper while being honest that the *verification step* depends on an outside prover the user must install. Jet's front end still owns the diagnostic (I2): a failed/timed-out proof is a Jet error, never solver output leaked to the user. This is post-Epoch research: the verification-condition generator, the spec language, trust in the bridge, and solver-output translation are each large. Cost: highest complexity, real external dependency for the prove step, and the spec language is a second surface to design carefully so it doesn't fork the type system.

comparisons.note: Verification-aware language: you write requires/ensures specs and Dafny discharges them via Z3 at compile time; verification is mandatory and the solver is core, not opt-in. Jet can't adopt this default-on model — it would put an SMT solver in every build (I6/beginner-path violation). Closest to Option C but without the expert gate.
comparisons.code:
method CtEq(a: array<byte>, b: array<byte>) returns (r: bool)
  requires a.Length == b.Length
  ensures r == (forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> a[i] == b[i])
{ ... }  // Z3 proves the ensures or the build fails

comparisons.note: Subset of Ada with contracts proved by an external prover (GNATprove/Why3); proof is opt-in per unit and layered (stone->gold->platinum). This is the closest precedent for Jet's Option C: a safe language where formal proof is an explicit, gated tier over normal compilation rather than the default — exactly the 'never in the default path' shape.

Bolt-on verifiers, none in rustc itself: Kani is a bounded model checker (finite unrolling — directly the Option B flavor), Prusti/Creusot are deductive SMT-backed (Option C flavor). All are separate opt-in tools you install and invoke, never part of `cargo build`. Validates that the foundational/bounded subset and the heavy prover can be cleanly separated, and that the prover lives outside the core toolchain.

Full dependently-typed proof assistants: maximal power (functional-correctness proofs, used for HACL* verified crypto), maximal cost — proofs are part of the source and the checker IS the compiler. This is beyond even Option C; cited to mark the far end of the gradient and why Jet would never embed a proof assistant in Source/ (it would BE an external proof kernel, the sharpest I6 collision).
comparisons.code:
let ct_eq (a b: bytes) : Pure bool
  (requires length a == length b)
  (ensures fun r -> r <==> equal a b) = ...
(* the F* typechecker discharges this; the proof ships with the code *)

decisions.title: Should Jet express resource/time budgets as types and statically warn when a called function exceeds them — and if so, in what form?
decisions.gist: A render-frame loop wants a 16ms CPU budget that the compiler can enforce. But sound static timing/cost inference (WCET) is research-grade and undecidable in general — you cannot prove a wall-clock bound from source. The honest split: decline it as a type, ship a foundational #Budget that is really an effect/capability ceiling (forbid known-expensive effects in a hot region), or commit to full RAML-style cost inference as a post-Epoch research track.
decisions.explainer: Real timing budgets are a runtime property of a specific machine, inputs, and cache state; proving a 16ms bound at compile time is the worst-case-execution-time (WCET) problem, which is undecidable in general and, where tractable, requires whole-program loop-bound annotations and a hardware cost model (Ada/SPARK + aiT, RAML's amortized analysis). None of that is an Epoch-3 feature, and none of it composes with I8 without inventing a parallel mechanism. The pragmatic insight: most frame-budget blowups in practice come from doing forbidden *kinds* of work in a hot path — heap allocation, IO, syscalls, unbounded loops. Jet already has the exact machinery to forbid effect categories in a region (#(…) bounds, #Caps(…) ceilings, E0740/E0741). A #Budget region is therefore not a timing proof at all — it is an effect ceiling with a cost-oriented name that bans Alloc/Io/Net and flags unbounded loops, giving real, sound guarantees (no allocation in the render path) without claiming a millisecond it cannot honor. Full cost inference (option C) stays an honest research item; the runtime deadline path (option A's pointer to D-DEADLINE1) is the sanctioned way to get actual wall-clock enforcement today.
decisions.story: I'm writing render_frame for a 60fps game and I keep blowing my 16ms budget because some helper deep in the call graph quietly allocates and hits the filesystem to lazy-load a texture. I want the compiler to tell me — at the call site, before I ship — that this hot path is doing something it must never do, instead of finding it in a profiler at 11fps.

options.name: Decline budgets-as-types — sanction the runtime path (D-DEADLINE1)
options.detail: Do not add any budget type or marker.
