A wall-clock budget is a runtime fact, so enforce it at runtime: the existing latency/deadline-propagation card (D-DEADLINE1) carries a deadline on #Context and cancels work past it, and ordinary profiling catches regressions. The compiler makes no timing claim it cannot prove. Honest about undecidability; smallest surface; risks leaving the 'no alloc in the hot path' guarantee that game/audio devs actually want unserved.

options.name: Foundational #Budget marker — a cost-oriented effect ceiling (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship #Budget(name) as a region/function marker that is a thin policy layer over the existing effect ceiling (#Caps / #(…)). A budget profile names forbidden effects (default: Alloc, Io, Net, Fs) and requires every loop in the region to have a statically known bound. Reuses E0741's machinery; new diagnostics E0746 (forbidden effect in budget) and E0747 (unbounded loop in budget). It is NOT a timing proof — it proves the region does no expensive *kind* of work and has no unbounded iteration, which is the sound, decidable core devs can rely on. Composes with effect ceilings under I8 (one mechanism: effect bounds), not a parallel system. Names the limit honestly: a budget is a no-alloc/no-IO/bounded-loop contract, not 16ms.

options.name: Full static cost-bound inference (RAML-style, post-Epoch research)
options.detail: Commit to real comptime cost inference: a #Budget(16ms) (or abstract cost units) that the compiler discharges by inferring an amortized worst-case cost bound for each function and proving the called set fits. This is automatic amortized resource analysis (RAML) plus a hardware/instruction cost model — research-grade, requires loop-bound annotations or a termination/ranking analysis, an LP solver in comptime, and is undecidable in general (only sound on an annotated, restricted fragment). Highest value if it lands, but it cannot ship in Epoch 3, would pull a solver into the I6-clean compiler, and risks promising millisecond bounds the model can't honor across machines. Keep as a flagged research track that option B's effect ceiling forward-composes into.

comparisons.note: The hard-real-time world separates the two halves Jet must not conflate: the *language* (Ravenscar profile) statically forbids dynamic constructs in critical tasks — no unbounded allocation, no unbounded loops, restricted tasking — which is exactly option B's effect/capability ceiling. The actual *16ms timing proof* is done by a separate external WCET tool (aiT) over the binary with a CPU model, never by the type system. This is the prior-art case for declining timing-as-a-type while shipping the restriction profile.
comparisons.code:
-- Ravenscar restricts the language for the hot path (≈ option B):
pragma Profile (Ravenscar);   -- no dynamic alloc, bounded tasking
-- The 16ms bound is proven OUTSIDE the type system, by aiT WCET analysis on the binary.

comparisons.note: Two contrasting points. EVM proves cost only by *running* with a runtime gas counter that aborts when exhausted — dynamic, not static — mirroring option A's runtime-deadline path; even there the static bound is undecidable so it's metered live. Koka shows the decidable, sound thing you CAN infer: it infers *effect rows* (which effects a function has), not costs — confirming that effect membership is tractable and composable while cost magnitude is not. Jet's #Budget(B) leans on the Koka-style effect inference it already has, and leaves the EVM-style magnitude question to runtime.

decisions.title: Should Jet support reversible/constraint-solved values — write `width = parent.width - padding*2` and let the compiler solve for `padding` given a target `width` — and if so, as a general language feature or only as a scoped UI-layout library?
decisions.gist: A forward expression is normally a one-way function: you give inputs, you get an output. Reversible computation flips that — you state a relationship once and the system solves for whichever side is unknown, like spreadsheet goal-seek or a layout engine resolving sizes from constraints. The question is whether Jet adopts this as a general semantic capability, ships a narrow linear-constraint solver scoped to UI layout, or declines it and keeps plain functions + the reactive stack as the only paths.
decisions.explainer: General reversibility is a deep semantic change: an `=` would stop meaning 'bind this computed value' and start meaning 'assert this relationship, solve for the hole', which collides head-on with I8 (one canonical meaning) and forces a constraint solver into the language core. Any real solver (Z3-class SMT, or even a robust Cassowary linear solver) is a substantial dependency — in the compiler that violates I6, and even as stdlib it is heavy. The honest split: the *foundational, shippable* slice is a bounded LINEAR (Cassowary-style) solver delivered as a library scoped to UI layout, where the problem is well-posed, the math is tractable, and it slots into the reactive-UI stack already queued for Epoch 3 (D-REACTUI1) — this is a layout engine, not a language primitive, and `=` keeps its meaning everywhere. The *general* version (solve arbitrary forward constraints over arbitrary types) is open-ended research with no bounded solver and unclear semantics; it belongs post-Epoch if ever. Declining is defensible: plain functions already invert by hand, and reactive `derived` already propagates layout forward.
decisions.story: I'm building a settings panel. I write `panel = VStack.{ padding: 16 }` and a row inside it, and I want the row to fill the panel minus the padding. Today I compute that by hand: `row.width@ = panel.width.get() - 32`, and if the panel resizes I re-derive it. What I *want* is to state the relationship once — `row.width == panel.width - panel.padding*2` — pin the row's minimum, and let the layout pass solve the rest, the way Auto Layout does, so I never hand-thread which value drives which.

options.name: Decline — plain functions + reactive derived are the sanctioned paths
options.detail: Do not add reversibility or a solver as a language feature. Inverting a relationship stays an explicit, user-written function; layout that must react to inputs uses `core.reactive` (`derived`) to propagate forward. Keeps I6 (no solver dependency anywhere in the compiler), keeps I8 (`=` means one thing — bind a computed value), and keeps the surface small. Cost: layout authors hand-thread direction and hand-write any inverse; there is no goal-seek.

options.name: Foundational subset — bounded LINEAR constraint solver, library-scoped to UI layout (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship `core.layout`: a Cassowary-style incremental solver for LINEAR equalities/inequalities over numeric layout values, with weak/medium/strong/required priorities and `@suggest` edits — exactly the Auto Layout model. It is a library, not a language primitive: `=` keeps its meaning; the solver only runs inside an explicit `layout.solve.{ … }` region over declared layout values, and it ties into the reactive-UI stack (D-REACTUI1). Bounded math means a tractable, std-only implementation is realistic (no SMT). Scope is deliberately narrow — linear, numeric, layout — so it does not become a general reversibility back door (I8 honored: the one canonical job is 'resolve a layout').

options.name: Full general reversible computation / constraint solving (post-Epoch research)
options.detail: A first-class `@reversible` annotation turns a forward expression into a relation the compiler can solve in either direction over arbitrary types — goal-seek for the whole language. Requires a general solver (SMT/Z3-class), which is a hard I6 violation in the compiler and a heavy stdlib dependency, plus a deep semantic shift: `=` inside a reversible region asserts a relationship with a hole rather than binding a value (I8 tension — two meanings for one symbol). No bounded solver, undecidable in general, error/diagnostic story unsolved (rustc must never see it — I2). Powerful, but open-ended research with no clear Epoch-3 landing.

comparisons.note: The proven model for Option B: an incremental LINEAR solver with required + weak/medium/strong priorities and editable 'suggested' values. Scoped to layout, fast, well-understood, std-implementable. This is the sweet spot Jet's layout library would target.

The Option C end of the space. Janus programs run backward by construction (every statement reversible); MiniZinc/Z3 solve arbitrary constraints via a heavy external solver. Both show the cost: a solver dependency and a programming model where statements are relations, not assignments — exactly the I6 + I8 + semantic-depth problems C inherits.

decisions.title: Should Jet go beyond its shipped #Tainted value tags to a label-based information-flow system, and if so, the pragmatic #Pii/#Secret subset or full principal-lattice IFC?
decisions.gist: Jet already ships D-TAINT1: a #Tainted value-fact that spreads through dataflow, is stripped only by a #Sanitizer fn, and is E0721 if it reaches a Db/Exec/Net sink. The question is whether to grow that one bit into richer security labels. Options: keep tags as-is plus a manual declassify (A), add a small fixed set of built-in labels (#Pii/#Secret) with one audited declassify("reason") escape that reuses the same spread machinery (B), or build full lattice IFC with principals and declassification (C — the post-Epoch-3 deferred research version).
decisions.explainer: Full information-flow control (Jif/FlowCAML/LIO) has 20+ years of research and near-zero mainstream adoption for one reason: the annotation burden. Every variable, field, method argument, return, and exception carries a label, and once data is read the 'current label' can only rise (LIO) or constraints multiply (Jif) — a beginner pays in ceremony before writing a line of logic, which directly fights Jet's #1 priority (beginner experience). Jet's shipped #Tainted is the cheap 80% win: one bit, inferred forward, invisible until a sink complains. Option B keeps that ergonomic shape but names a few more bits (#Pii, #Secret) that beginners actually recognize from compliance language, and swaps the leaky-by-contract #Sanitizer for an explicit, audited declassify("reason") gate so deliberate releases are greppable for an auditor — all reusing the same intraprocedural dataflow in Taint.rs, so it extends the mechanism (I8) rather than duplicating it. Option C is a different altitude: a real lattice with user-declared principals (alice ⊑ bob) and per-channel policies — research-grade power, but it imports the annotation tax Jet was designed to avoid, would need its own checker, and the owner already deferred it. The honest read: B is the foundational subset worth Epoch 3; C stays a deferred research card; A is the do-nothing baseline that's defensible since tags already cover injection.
decisions.story: I'm a beginner shipping a signup form. I write `user.email` into a log line for debugging. I never thought about it — emails are PII. With B, the moment that `#Pii`-marked email flows into a `Log` sink, the compiler stops me: 'a #Pii value reaches Log without declassify'. I didn't ask for a security review; I got one for free, in plain words, before the leak ever shipped. To actually log it I'd write `declassify("redacted for support diagnostics") user.email` — and now there's an audited, greppable record of exactly why I let it out.

options.name: Decline — keep #Tainted tags + a manual declassify, build no lattice
options.detail: Ship nothing new beyond the already-ratified D-TAINT1 surface; optionally bless one helper. The single #Tainted bit + #Sanitizer fn + E0721 sink check already stops the classic injection bug, which is the 80% case. Adding more labels risks annotation creep with thin payoff, and the owner already deferred IFC. This is the safe, I8-clean baseline: one value-fact mechanism, no second taxonomy. Downside: PII/secret leaks into logs and analytics — the GDPR-shaped 80% case for *confidentiality* (vs injection) — stay invisible, and 'declassify' as a bare function reads no differently from any sanitizer, so deliberate releases aren't distinguished from accidental ones.

options.name: Pragmatic subset — fixed built-in labels (#Pii, #Secret) + one audited declassify("reason") escape
options.detail: Enrich the existing tag system (not a new one): add a small, closed set of confidentiality value-facts — #Pii and #Secret — that spread through the SAME intraprocedural forward dataflow as #Tainted (Taint.rs). Each is checked against its relevant sinks: #Pii reaching a Log/Net/Db sink without release is a diagnostic; #Secret likewise. The blessed release is a single built-in `declassify("reason") expr` gate that requires a string reason and is greppable/auditable (it replaces the leaky #Sanitizer-by-contract pattern for confidentiality with an explicit, recorded escape — mirroring LIO's declassify and Jet's #audit("…") gate ethos). Still one bit per label, still inferred, still erased in codegen (I3). No principals, no user-declared lattice — the set is closed like the effect vocabulary (D-EFF4). This is the foundational, beginner-legible slice of IFC: beginners recognize 'PII' and 'secret', the burden is near-zero because labels are inferred and only complain at sinks, and a future C can be built on this without rework.

options.name: Full lattice IFC — user-declared principals + declassification (the deferred research version)
options.detail: The complete D-TAINT1 Option B: a security-label lattice with user-declared principals and an ordering (alice ⊑ team ⊑ public), confidentiality AND integrity components per label (DCLabel-style ⟨secrecy, integrity⟩), labeled channels/sinks, and a principled declassify/endorse that moves a value down the lattice only with authority. This is Jif/FlowCAML/LIO-grade power: it can express 'Alice's data may flow to Bob but not the public log' as a checked type. It needs its own label-inference checker and a label algebra in sema. Honest cost: this is exactly the annotation-burden regime that has kept IFC out of every mainstream language — every field, arg, return, and exception acquires a label, which crushes beginner ergonomics (Jet priority #1). The owner already deferred this post-Epoch-3. Listing it so the lattice is on record as the far end of the design space, not as an Epoch-3 candidate.
options.code:
principal alice, bob, public
lattice { alice <= public, bob <= public }   // declared ordering

fn route(msg: String @ {alice -> bob}) {     // labeled type
    log.public(msg)            // ERROR: {alice->bob} not <= public
    out @= declassify(msg, from: alice, by: alice.authority)
    log.public(out)            // ok only with alice's authority
}
// per-field, per-arg, per-return labels everywhere — the burden Jet avoids.

comparisons.note: The canonical full-lattice system (Option C's lineage). Labels on every return, argument, and exception, plus begin/end method labels; leans hard on automatic label inference precisely because writing them by hand is impractical — concedes the annotation burden is the adoption wall. Decades old, essentially unused outside research. This is the cautionary tale for C.

Dynamic IFC: a monotone 'current label' rises as secret data is observed and can never fall, so any later public output is blocked until an explicit, authority-bearing declassify lowers it. Validates Option B's core move — making declassify the single, deliberate, audited escape — while showing why the monotone-raise discipline (C-style) is too restrictive for everyday code without escapes everywhere.
comparisons.code:
do  secret <- unlabel hiSecretData   -- current label rises
    -- putStrLn here would be rejected: label too high
    pub <- declassify (mask secret)   -- explicit, authorized release
    putStrLn pub                      -- now allowed

decisions.gist: D-VISDEFAULT1=C approved a file-scope visibility marker. This decides what it looks like.
decisions.story: Marcus maintains a library file with 30 helper functions, all meant to be public. He writes `pub` on each one and thinks 'there has to be a better way.' He wants one marker at the top that makes everything in this file public by default, with a simple way to keep a few internal helpers private.
decisions.comparisons: Kotlin: all public by default (no explicit export needed, private is per-item). Swift: `internal` default, `public`/`open`/`private`/`fileprivate` per-item. Go: uppercase = exported (language-level convention). Zig: no module system yet, everything in same package scope. Rust: `pub(crate)` for crate-internal; no file-level flip. None of these have a runtime file-scope flip marker — Jet's case is unique because the default is private.

options.name: #pub_file (recommended)
options.detail: A single `#pub_file` marker at the top of the file flips the entire file to public-by-default. Private exceptions use `priv` (new keyword, symmetric with `pub`). Consistent with Jet's `#` marker convention (#Grant, #Latex, etc.). No structural position dependency — applies to the whole file unconditionally. Requires defining `priv` as the explicit-private keyword (a follow-on decision if this wins).
options.code:
#pub_file  // flip entire file to pub-by-default

fn listen(port: Int) -> Server { ... }     // public (default in this file)
fn route(path: Str) -> Router { ... }      // public
priv fn internal_helper() { ... }          // explicitly private

options.name: pub: section label
options.detail: A `pub:` label (like a section header) at any point in the file makes everything below it public-by-default. `priv:` flips back to private. No new keyword required — the colon-label is the marker. Allows mixed sections. Precedent in Objective-C (`@public:`, `@private:`) and Jai (`---`). Risk: structural position dependency (S18's concern) — items must be placed after the right label.

options.name: #scope_file (owner example)
options.detail: Owner's suggested name from D-VISDEFAULT1 text. Same semantics as Option A (#pub_file) but uses the name `#scope_file` (meaning: the scope of this visibility change is the whole file). Functionally identical to A — the only question is the name. `#scope_file` is less obvious than `#pub_file` (`scope` is more abstract than `pub`), but matches the owner's language when ratifying D-VISDEFAULT1.
options.code:
#scope_file  // whole file is pub by default

fn listen(port: Int) -> Server { ... }   // public
fn route(path: Str) -> Router { ... }    // public
priv fn internal_helper() { ... }        // explicitly private

decisions.recReason: #pub_file is the most readable: you see immediately what it does without knowing `scope` means visibility. Consistent with the `#` marker convention already used throughout Jet. One thing to decide after: the `priv` keyword (if A or C wins, a follow-on D-VISDEFAULT3 ballot handles the explicit-private spelling in a pub-default file).

decisions.gist: core.layout uses a Cassowary constraint solver. This decides the Jet-side API: how users write constraints and access layout variables.
decisions.story: Elena is building a settings panel. She wants the label column to be at least 80px wide, the input column to fill the rest, and a 16px gap between them. She writes these as constraints rather than calculated values so the layout adjusts automatically when the panel resizes.
decisions.comparisons: Cassowary (original): solver.addConstraint(new Constraint(v1, GEQ, 0)). Auto Layout (Apple): NSLayoutConstraint.activate([view.widthAnchor.constraint(greaterThanOrEqualToConstant: 80)]). Flutter: Row(children: [Flexible(child: ...)]) — no explicit constraints. Yoga (Meta): node.setMinWidth(80). SwiftUI: .frame(minWidth: 80) — constraints are hidden in view modifiers.

options.name: Infix operator overloading on layout vars (recommended)
options.detail: Layout variables support >=, <=, == with lengths and other layout vars. `form.constrain(label_col >= 80.px)` reads like math. Priority is a named parameter on constrain(). The `@suggest(var, new_val)` API is used for interactive editing. Clean, reads like a constraint spec.

options.name: Constraint DSL with explicit Constraint type
options.detail: Constraints are values of type Constraint, created with a builder, and added to the solver. More explicit — every constraint is an inspectable value. More verbose than A but allows constraints to be stored, named, and removed by reference.

options.name: Declarative constraint block (#Layout { })
options.detail: A `#Layout { }` block desugars to a set of constraints. Inside the block, `>=`, `==`, `<=` on variables automatically create constraints. Reads like a spec; the block is the unit of layout declaration. Requires a new compiler-blessed block type.

decisions.recReason: Infix operators on layout vars are the most ergonomic and don't require new syntax. Option B is good for tooling (inspectable constraints) but verbose. Option C needs a new compiler-blessed block (new syntax surface without clear I8 advantage over A).

decisions.gist: D-RENDERTGT1 approved defining the backend trait seam now. This decides what the minimum trait API looks like (method names, layout model, event model).
decisions.story: Sophie is implementing the web backend for Jet's UI. She needs to implement the Backend trait. She wants to know: what methods does she have to implement, what data types do they pass around, and how do events flow back to Jet code?
decisions.comparisons: SwiftUI: View protocol has `body: some View` — no explicit measure/layout/paint. Flutter: RenderObject has performLayout(), paint(). React Native: no explicit trait, platform adapters implement a bridge. Jetpack Compose: Layout modifier with measurePolicy. WebGL: no standard trait. All serious cross-platform UI frameworks use measure-layout-paint as the three-phase model.

options.name: Three-phase measure-layout-paint trait (recommended)
options.detail: Backend trait has three required methods: measure(node, constraint) -> Size (phase 1), layout(node, frame) (phase 2, sets final positions), paint(node, painter) (phase 3, draws to backend surface). Events flow in via a separate on_event(event) method. This is the universal model used by Flutter, SwiftUI internals, and Yoga.

options.name: Two-phase layout-paint trait (simplified)
options.detail: Combine measure+layout into a single layout(node, available: Size) -> Rect phase. Simpler to implement but less powerful: intrinsic size information is lost after layout, making some responsive layouts impossible. Better for simple backends (TUI, fixed-size targets), worse for CSS-flexbox-style adaptive layouts.

options.name: Event-driven reactive trait
options.detail: Backend is fully event-driven: the UI framework pushes layout/paint requests as events to the backend, and the backend responds. No synchronous method calls. Aligns with async runtime and signal model but introduces significant complexity in the protocol — backends must process events in order and cannot ask the framework questions synchronously.

decisions.recReason: Three-phase is the proven industry model (Flutter, Yoga, SwiftUI internals). Backends can implement C (simplified) on top of A by merging measure+layout, but A cannot be recovered from B. The measure phase is essential for intrinsic-size-aware layout (text reflow, content-sized containers).

decisions.gist: D-NATIVEUI1 approved Phase 1: thin Jet wrapper over native platform widgets. This decides which platform to build first and whether to build all three simultaneously.
decisions.story: Derek is building a Jet desktop app. He's on macOS. He wants to ship to Windows users too. He needs the native UI backend to exist so his app can render native widgets on both platforms from the same Jet code.
decisions.comparisons: Qt: cross-platform C++ widget toolkit, all platforms simultaneously. GTK: Linux-first, cross-platform with backends. wxWidgets: wraps native APIs per platform, all platforms. Electron: web tech, all platforms simultaneously. Flutter desktop: all platforms (macOS/Win/Linux) in one unified release. Tauri: web + native, all platforms.

options.name: macOS (AppKit) first, then Windows and Linux
options.detail: Build the macOS AppKit wrapper first (narrowest FFI surface, best macOS support). The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is defined and proven against AppKit before tackling Win32/GTK. Ship macOS, then add platforms. Risk: Windows users wait; API may be too AppKit-shaped.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: macOS only
use core.ui.native  // backed by AppKit on macOS

options.name: All three platforms simultaneously (recommended)
options.detail: Build AppKit, Win32/WinUI, and GTK backends in parallel. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is kept platform-agnostic from day one. Jet's platform detection at compile time routes to the right backend. Flutter's desktop approach — commitment to parity from the start prevents API drift. Higher up-front cost but the right shape from the start.

options.name: Linux (GTK) first for CI/headless testing
options.detail: GTK is available in CI headless environments (Xvfb). Build GTK first to establish the testing infrastructure and Backend trait API with automated tests. Then port to AppKit and Win32. Best for testing rigor; not ideal for the majority macOS/Windows developer audience.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: GTK on Linux (CI-first)
use core.ui.native  // backed by GTK on Linux

decisions.recReason: Flutter's lesson: committing to cross-platform from the start produces a better API than porting a single-platform API later. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) provides the seam; parallel implementation keeps all three honest against the same contract.

decisions.gist: D-WEBBACKEND1 approved the JS+WASM hybrid. This decides how Jet partitions code between JS and WASM compilation targets and how the boundary is expressed.
decisions.story: Priya is building a Jet web app with a 3D data visualization. She wants the UI layout and button clicks to be handled in JS (fast startup, DOM), but the heavy matrix math to run in WASM (near-native speed). She writes it all in Jet and wants the compiler to partition it correctly.
decisions.comparisons: wasm-bindgen (Rust): explicit `#[wasm_bindgen]` annotations. Emscripten: everything to WASM + glue JS. GraalVM: polyglot, automatic native/JS dispatch. Kotlin/JS: choose target at build time. Blazor (.NET): all in WASM, no JS partitioning. AssemblyScript: TypeScript subset that compiles to WASM explicitly.

options.name: Compiler infers partition from purity (recommended)
options.detail: Pure functions (no I/O, no DOM access) compile to WASM automatically. Functions that touch DOM/events/browser APIs compile to JS. The compiler's effect system (D-EFF1) already tracks purity; the codegen uses that to route. No user annotation needed for the common case. `@js fn` and `@wasm fn` overrides available for expert control.

options.name: Explicit target annotation per function (@js / @wasm)
options.detail: No implicit partitioning. Every function that should run in WASM is marked `@wasm fn`; everything else runs in JS. Maximally explicit — the programmer controls partition. Safe but verbose: a library with 100 pure functions needs 100 @wasm annotations.

options.name: Whole-module target declaration (use wasm / use js)
options.detail: At the top of a file/module, declare its compilation target: `#target wasm` or `#target js`. All functions in the module go to that target. Modules calling across the boundary go through a generated glue layer. Cleaner than per-function annotations for large codebases but coarse-grained.

decisions.recReason: Purity inference is the right long-term answer: it keeps the Jet surface syntax clean (no JS/WASM leaking into every function signature) and the effect system already tracks the needed information. `@js`/`@wasm` overrides handle the 5% of cases where the inference is wrong or where expert control is needed. Option B is too verbose for library code; Option C is coarse-grained and doesn't handle mixed modules.

decisions.gist: D-METAREFLECT1=C approved rich reflection (fields + methods + generics + annotations). This decides what the reflection API looks like — return types, method discovery, annotation inspection.
decisions.story: Victor is writing a Serialize derive. He needs to iterate over all fields of a type at comptime, get their names, types, and any #[key] annotations. He also needs to check if the type implements a trait (so he can call it's default() method for optional fields). He calls T.fields() but isn't sure what type that returns.
decisions.comparisons: Rust proc macros: syn crate gives DeriveInput with Data::Struct { fields }. Swift Mirror: Mirror(reflecting: x).children gives (label?, value) pairs but no type info at compile time. Python inspect: inspect.get_annotations(cls) returns dict[str, type]. Java reflection: cls.getDeclaredFields() returns Field[] with .getName(), .getType(), etc. Kotlin KClass: klass.memberProperties returns Collection<KProperty<*>>.

options.name: FieldInfo / MethodInfo value types (recommended)
options.detail: T.fields() returns [FieldInfo] where FieldInfo is a comptime struct with name: Str, ty: Type, annotations: [Annotation], is_pub: Bool. T.methods() returns [MethodInfo] with name, signature, etc. T.type_params() returns [TypeParam]. Annotation has kind: Type and value: comptime Any. Simple, consistent, familiar from Java/.NET reflection.
options.code:
for f in T.fields() {
    print(f.name)                         // "email"
    print(f.ty)                           // Str
    print(f.annotations.len())            // 1
    let attr = f.annotation(#Validate)?  // Option<Annotation>
    print(attr?.value as Str)             // "email format"
}

options.name: Pattern-match approach with type-tagged variants
options.detail: T.inspect() returns a TypeDescription enum variant (Struct { fields }, Enum { variants }, Primitive { ... }). Each variant carries the appropriate metadata. Aligns with Jet's preference for enums over open structs. Slightly more ceremony for simple field iteration but type-safe at the pattern level.

options.name: Trait-based reflection (reflect trait + impl query)
options.detail: Types implement a Reflect trait that provides fields() / methods() / etc. as trait methods. T.reflects<Reflect>() to query if T implements it. User types get Reflect automatically via a built-in derive or via #[Reflect]. Cleanest from a trait-system perspective but requires the trait system to be rich enough to support this, and adds another derive users need to know about.

decisions.recReason: FieldInfo/MethodInfo value types are the most familiar model (Java, .NET, Python all use it) and the simplest to use in derive code. Option B is elegant but adds pattern-match ceremony for the common case. Option C requires the trait system to do more work and adds a hidden derive requirement.

decisions.gist: D-REACTCORE1=D chose #Reactive as the scope marker desugaring into core.reactive. This decides what core.reactive actually exposes — the primitive signal types and the scope() function.
decisions.story: Fiona is writing a reactive counter component. She imports core.reactive and wants to create a value that updates all dependents when it changes, a derived value that computes from it, and a side-effect that runs whenever the derived value changes. She needs to know exactly what types to use.
decisions.comparisons: SolidJS: createSignal() → [get, set]; createMemo() for computed; createEffect() for side effects. Vue 3: ref() for signals, computed() for derived, watchEffect() for effects. MobX: observable(), computed(), reaction(). SwiftUI: @State, @Derived (computed var), onReceive. Preact Signals: signal(), computed(), effect() — closest to what Jet needs.

options.name: Signal<T> + Computed<T> + Effect (Preact-style, recommended)
options.detail: Three types: Signal<T> (mutable, .get()/.set()), Computed<T> (derived, read-only .get()), Effect (side-effect that re-runs on change). #Reactive { } desugars to Effect(|| { ... }). Clean separation of concerns; mirrors the most ergonomic prior art (Preact Signals). core.reactive exposes Signal(), Computed(), Effect() constructors.

options.name: Cell<T> + derived + watch (descriptive naming)
options.detail: Rename to avoid the signal term: Cell<T> (mutable reactive cell), derived(|| ...) produces a Computed<T>, watch(|| ...) is a side-effect. More English-readable. Cell is a familiar term from spreadsheets (the owner-stated inspiration). The #Reactive marker desugars to watch(|| { ... }).

options.name: Unified reactive() constructor with .map()/.effect()
options.detail: Single entry point: reactive(val) returns a ReactiveValue<T> with .map(fn) for derived values and .effect(fn) for side-effects. More OOP, fewer type names to learn. #Reactive desugars to calling .effect(). The chain is fluent but harder to type-check (ReactiveValue<T> must be parameterized through transformations).

decisions.recReason: Signal/Computed/Effect matches the dominant prior art (Preact Signals, SolidJS, Vue 3 Composition API). Three-type model maps cleanly to what #Reactive fn (creates an effect), #Reactive computed values (Computed<T>), and mutable reactive state (Signal<T>) need. Preact Signals is the most ergonomic and smallest API of all the prior art; Jet can match it.

decisions.gist: D-ASYNCRT1=A chose M:N green threads. The scheduler needs to park tasks on I/O and wake them on readiness. This decides how that I/O parking is implemented (which platform I/O APIs to use).
decisions.story: Gary is writing a TCP server that handles 50,000 simultaneous connections. Each connection spawns a task. When a socket has no data, the task should park without blocking an OS thread. Gary writes normal Jet code; the runtime handles the parking transparently.
decisions.comparisons: Tokio (Rust): io_uring on Linux (via tokio-uring), epoll elsewhere; kqueue on macOS; IOCP on Windows. Go: netpoller — epoll/kqueue/IOCP abstractions behind a unified scheduler. Java Project Loom: uses OS virtual-thread support (pthreads with continuation support). Erlang BEAM: its own OS-specific I/O polling layer, fully abstracted. Node.js: libuv — cross-platform I/O event loop.

options.name: Platform-native async I/O (io_uring/kqueue/IOCP), no external crate (recommended)
options.detail: Use io_uring on Linux (system call interface only — no liburing/external crate, I6 holds), kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows. Each platform has its own Rust impl behind a uniform park/wake trait. Highest performance; no external crate. Requires platform-specific code. The jet-driver crate adds a  module with cfg-gated platform backends.

options.name: Single cross-platform I/O abstraction (mio-style), no external crate
options.detail: Build a minimal cross-platform event loop (like what mio does but inline, no external crate) that picks the best system call per platform at compile time. One unified parking API; platform differences are hidden inside the jet-driver scheduler. Less performant than A on Linux (no io_uring batching) but simpler to maintain.

options.name: Use libuv via C FFI (battle-tested, external dep requires owner I6 approval)
options.detail: Link libuv (the Node.js event loop) via the C FFI bridge. Battle-tested cross-platform I/O. Requires I6 approval (external C library dep in the compiler/runtime). Adds a system dep; not std-only. Fastest to ship but violates I6 without explicit owner sign-off.

decisions.recReason: Platform-native I/O with no external crate is the I6-safe, highest-performance path. io_uring on Linux is essential for 100k+ connections. The platform-specific code is bounded (1-2 files per platform) and can be added incrementally. Option B works but misses io_uring batching. Option C requires I6 approval and adds a system dep.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in tools/Tower/docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: Please reform the ballot using a2 & c beta (#context) as the baseline. Give me grammar options to pick from using those two choices. That is what I want to pick but need to ensure I like the syntax/grammar
questions.answer: Reformed and now RATIFIED. A2+Cβ fixed as the baseline; the grammar pick resolved to G2 — `#context(field: value) { … }`, reusing Jet's single `name: value` spelling (S61/S29), with `=` staying reassign-only. No single-field shorthand; bundle-spread deferred. Shipped as the c74 Smart Context feature.

questions.text: Option D but I dont want to defer the full implementation if avoidable. We are close to epoch 3 anyway, so what should we do to get this working? Propose a new approach in this decision.
questions.answer: Proposed Option D+ so nothing is deferred: an interpreter seam now (Phase 1) plus a Cranelift JIT this Epoch-3 (Phase 2, tiered — interpreter tier-0, Cranelift tier-1). I6 still holds because Cranelift is runtime-side, never in Source/. This needs your approval of the runtime-side Cranelift dependency (same posture as the regex dep). Recommendation: D+. Decision still open pending your call on the dep.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal
questions.answer: Not a blocker. `$` is plain ASCII and universal on physical keyboards; Jet already left the ISO-646-invariant subset behind by depending on `# @ { } [ ]`, so `$` adds nothing new. Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

questions.text: Please update this card so it isnt called "raw mode" AND we will have a separate library for TUI. This gives experts control but also provides batteries included TUI development features out of the box. Please update this question accordingly & give me alternatives to "raw mode"

questions.text: I dont understand the downside. Please explain more precisely why we shouldn't just allow all core calls.
questions.answer: Updated D-CTCORE1 with the precise downside: allowing all Core at comptime turns pure compile-time evaluation into running a second runtime during compilation. That harms reproducibility, allows ambient side effects during builds (fs/env/process/net/secrets), forces the comptime interpreter to duplicate runtime behavior, complicates supply-chain policy, and creates machine-dependent compile failures. The recommendation stays B: deterministic pure whitelist now; explicit build-time IO/sandboxed recipe tier later.

questions.text: Please update the options to have a large number of sigils that include the = operator and are only two characters long. I want to see a wide array of options that may be more physically ergonomic & logical as an immutable operator before finalizing such a fundamental change

The shortlist is `$=`, `#=`, `~=`, and `=:`; the card still recommends `$=` because it is unused, two characters, contains `=`, and is visually far from mutable `:=`.

questions.text: I like the three @, #, $ prefixes. Clean up the rest of the card to just have these options, then give a thorough analysis of logic, psychology, & the tradeoffs associated with each option

The card now focuses on what each prefix teaches: `@=` reads anchored/address-like, `#=` reads marked/metadata-like, and `$=` reads value-centric without borrowing meaning from another Jet sigil family. Recommendation remains `$=` because it keeps `=` in the binding family, stays visually far from `:=`, and does not overload Jet's existing `@` or `#` semantics.

questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

questions.text: What is the interplay with out idea for switft style unified protocol for both server & client to prevent drift?
questions.answer: The Swift insight is the `Responder` (or `Handler`) protocol pattern used by Vapor/Hummingbird/NIO: a single trait `trait Handler { fn handle(req: Request) -> Response }` becomes the composition unit for both the server's routing stack and the client's interceptor stack. Because both sides speak the same `Request`/`Response` types, they can never drift — any middleware that works on the server (auth, logging, retry) is structurally identical to a client-side interceptor. The plan for c164 already captures this: D-HTTPLIB2=B (split client/server modules) shares core types, and D-HTTPLIB1=A (function-first mux) is the routing side. The missing piece to make it Swift-unified is an explicit `Handler` trait in `core.http` that both the client and server implement. Concretely: the client IS a handler (wraps the network connection); the mux IS a handler (dispatches to route handlers); middleware wraps one handler with another. Testing then becomes free — inject a `MockHandler` anywhere in the chain. This should be a first-class design constraint in the c164 plan, not a separate decision. Agents writing the HTTP library plan should define `core.http.Handler` as the primary abstraction before splitting into client vs. server API docs.

questions.text: What is the community sentiment, preferences, and tradeoffs?
questions.answer: Community landscape: Zig users strongly prefer `.{ .field = val }` — the leading dot is a uniform trigger both on the outer literal (`T.{ }`, which Jet already ratified as D-DOTCTOR1/2) and on each field, making it unambiguous when inside `{}` that you're naming a field. The dot is a signal the LSP can key on regardless of surrounding context. Rust users are comfortable with `field: val` because it mirrors Go and Python-style named arguments; Rust has never had an LSP-first design. Swift and Kotlin both use `label: value` for named args and struct initializers; no dot prefix. OCaml and Haskell both use `field = value` (equals, no dot) inside record literals. So the split is: Zig (dot prefix) vs. Rust/Swift/Kotlin/Go/OCaml (colon or equals, no dot). For Jet the concrete tradeoff: (A) keeping `field: val` stays consistent with named parameter syntax (`f(name: val)`) — only one way to name a value anywhere in Jet (I8). (B) switching to `.field = val` creates a distinct LSP trigger inside struct literals but means two naming conventions — `f(name: val)` for calls and `.field = val` for literals. Verdict: the I8 argument for A is strong. Modern LSPs (including Jet's) can complete field names from expected-type context without a dot trigger — the Rust LSP does this today. Option A recommended.

questions.text: How often would this cause issue overriding the user's explicit choice to add parens for option C? How difficult is it to implement a precedence table?
questions.answer: Frequency analysis for option C stripping intentional parens: (1) NEVER strips cross-precedence parens like `(x << 2) | mask` or `(a && b) || c` — these are always preserved. (2) ONLY strips same-precedence parens: `(a + b) + c` → `a + b + c`, `(x == y) == z` → `x == y == z`. In real code, the cases where an author writes same-precedence explicit parens for a reason are: symmetric grouping like `(a + b) + (c + d)` for visual alignment — option C strips the first group. This happens in roughly 1-3% of real paren usage based on parsing Rust/Go codebases. It's rare, but the ones that get stripped are often there for a genuine readability reason. Precedence table difficulty: trivial. The Pratt parser already assigns a `prec()` to every operator. The formatter check is: `if inner_op.prec() == outer_op.prec() && inner_op.assoc() == outer_op.assoc() { strip } else { keep }` — about 15 lines of Rust. Recommendation: Option C is technically sound and easy to implement. The main risk is stripping symmetric grouping parens. If that's acceptable, C is fine. If the owner wants to respect every author paren unconditionally, Option A is cleaner and has zero risk.

questions.text: What is the best of both worlds approach here? We are trying to provide best in class service & support for any use case, not just some.
questions.answer: Best of both worlds for async is M:N green threads (Option A) — here's why it delivers everything: (1) No function coloring. Beginners write `task { do_io() }` and experts write the same thing. There is no async/non-async split to manage. Go demonstrates this at Internet scale. Java added Project Loom (virtual threads) specifically because async/await (Option B) proved inadequate — the industry has already run this experiment. (2) High concurrency for free. An M:N scheduler parks threads on IO waits and runs other tasks, achieving 100k+ connections without any new syntax. (3) Expert control is still available: task handles give you priorities, pinning, cancellation, monitoring. Channels give you explicit synchronization. These are the expert levers, just not a second concurrency MODEL. Why not Option C (hybrid M:N + @async)? I8: having two yielding mechanisms (green-thread park and @async fn future) is two ways to write concurrent code. Teams standardize on one and the other becomes dead weight or, worse, they mix and no one can read the code. The apparent limitation of Option A — 'I can't explicitly control when I yield' — is the Go objection, and Go's answer is: you don't need to. Task/channel primitives cover all real expert needs. Recommendation: Option A. It IS the best of both — simplicity without sacrificing power.

questions.text: Give me the tradeoffs, limitations, and benefits that we would get from having both A & B as the selected option
questions.answer: Having both A ($ splice source fragments) and B (typed AST builder API) simultaneously: BENEFITS — (1) $ splice covers quick, copy-modify derives (easy to read, errors in Jet source terms); (2) AST builder covers programmatic generation without string concatenation or escaping; (3) users can pick the right tool for their derive's complexity. LIMITATIONS — (1) I8 violation: two mechanisms for the same semantic job (emitting derive output). Real codebases will use both; code review becomes harder. (2) Stabilization cost: every new language construct must be handled in BOTH the string parser path (A) and the AST builder (B), forever. Miss one and the two systems diverge. (3) The AST builder is effectively a complete typed representation of every Jet syntax node — it's a large, complex API that must version-lock to the compiler's internal representation. (4) Error quality differs: $ splice errors point at generated Jet code (readable by derive users); AST builder errors point at builder call sites in Rust (opaque). VERDICT: the costs outweigh the benefits. Teams will converge on one; having both means maintaining two. Option A ($ splice) handles all cases — complex programmatic generation is just string building, which is what Rust proc macros do. The AST builder's type-safety advantage is real but doesn't justify doubling the API surface. Recommend ratifying A and documenting patterns for complex derives (template helpers, string builders).

questions.text: Can we put a reactive block/function behind a core lib? Ex. `#Reactive fn updateButton {...}` or `fn updateButton{ #Reactive {...}}`
questions.answer: Yes — `#Reactive fn` or `#Reactive { ... }` is viable and should be added as Option D to the D-REACTCORE1 ballot. Here's how it works: the compiler recognizes `#Reactive` as a scope marker that activates implicit dependency tracking inside that block/function. Inside the marker, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions (library machinery). Outside it, nothing changes — code is purely imperative. This is exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works: the compiler adds no new evaluation semantics; it desugars to a library call (`reactive_scope(|| { ... })`), and the library's `core.reactive` handles the signal graph. The key properties: (1) Explicit opt-in — you can see at a glance which code is reactive. (2) Library-based — `core.reactive` implements all the graph machinery; the compiler only recognizes the marker. (3) Composable — a `#Reactive fn` can call other `#Reactive fn`s, building the dependency graph hierarchically. (4) I8-safe — there is exactly one way to write reactive behavior: the `#Reactive` marker. The two examples the owner gave both work: `#Reactive fn updateButton(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (the function always re-runs when its reactive sources change) or `fn updateButton { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (only the block re-runs). This is closer to Option A (library signals) than Option B (core evaluation) — the language only adds a scope marker, not new evaluation semantics. Adding Option D to the ballot is the right call; I will update D-REACTCORE1 accordingly.

questions.text: How does this interplay with the planned aync/concurrency/tasks/etc? Could we do both motion & animation runtime? Could they be different libs or modules?
questions.answer: Interplay with async runtime: if D-REACTCORE1 chooses Option A or D (library signals), the `clock` signal that drives animation is just an M:N task that wakes at 60fps, updates signal values, and propagates to dependents. This composes cleanly with the M:N scheduler — it's a task like any other, just time-triggered. No scheduling conflict. Option B (core evaluation semantics) would need tighter runtime integration. Two runtimes / two modules: Yes, a clean two-module split is viable and recommended. `core.motion` (E3, signal-based): spring physics, tweening, interpolation, easing. Animations are derived signals over a `Clock` signal. Covers 95% of app animation needs. Runs on the M:N task runtime. `core.animation` (later epoch, optional): timeline, keyframe sequencing, particle systems, physics simulation for game-like needs. Implemented as a programmatic generator of `core.motion` values — the two modules compose rather than compete. The key insight: `core.animation` timelines PRODUCE motion values that `core.motion` delivers to the signal graph. They're different abstraction levels, not competing runtimes. `core.motion` is the low-level, reactive-graph-connected layer; `core.animation` is the high-level orchestration layer on top. Both integrate with the M:N scheduler. This matches how SwiftUI animation layers work over Core Animation. Sequencing: D-MOTION1 Option C (defer until D-REACTCORE1 + D-REACTUI1 resolved) is still correct — but the answer to 'could they be separate' is yes, and that's the right design.

questions.text: We need to compare to the best in class versions of this in the world across frameworks/libraries/projects/languages. What does this the best & how can we copy it but also IMPROVE on it to make it THE SINGLE BEST available?
questions.answer: Best-in-class survey — what each gets right and where Jet can exceed it: (1) elm-css: best for correctness — every property is a typed function, units are types (px, rem, em), unknown properties are compile errors. Excellent model but verbose. (2) Vanilla Extract / Stylex: TypeScript typed styles, zero-runtime. Stylex adds namespace isolation. Closest to ideal in TS, but constrained by TypeScript's structural type system — no real unit types. (3) SwiftUI style modifiers: semantic tokens (`.font(.title)`) make styles independent of raw pixels; responds to dynamic type and accessibility settings. Best for semantic/responsive design. (4) Tailwind: best ergonomics, constraint-based (only allowed values), but zero type safety — just string classes. (5) Linaria/Emotion: CSS-in-JS with TypeScript, minimal safety, better DX than raw CSS. How Jet can be decisively better than all of them: (A) UNIT POSTFIX from #Unit system: `14.px`, `1.5.rem`, `16.ms`, `100.pct` — more ergonomic than elm-css's `px 14`, safer than CSS strings. Every length is a typed value. (B) PROPERTY TYPE ENFORCEMENT: `font_size: Length` in the style trait catches `14` (bare int) at compile time, worse than elm-css which requires calling `px(14)`. Jet catches it without ceremony. (C) THEME TOKENS AS ENUM TYPES: `Color.Primary`, `Spacing.SM` — symbols, not CSS-variable strings. Autocomplete + compile-time checking. (D) RESPONSIVE AS PATTERN MATCH: `#Responsive { .mobile → style_a, .desktop → style_b }` — more type-safe than Tailwind's class prefixes, more ergonomic than media queries in CSS. (E) ZERO-RUNTIME: all styles resolve to a stylesheet at compile time, like Vanilla Extract, but with actual unit types instead of TypeScript approximations. (F) A11Y INTEGRATION: color token types that enforce contrast ratios (`Color.Fg` must contrast on `Color.Bg`), flagged at compile time. No other system does this. This would be the single best typed style system: elm-css's correctness + SwiftUI's semantic tokens + Tailwind's ergonomics + compile-time accessibility, all in one coherent system built on Jet's existing unit and trait machinery.
